Article Title: Two Connecticut homeowners went to court in 2019 over a utility pole that prevented them from widening their driveway; seven years later, an appeals court upheld an order requiring neighbours to autho
Article Text:
A utility pole that stood in the way of two homeowners widening their driveway (AI image)

Why the pole became a problem

Disagreement over cost and removal method

Safety concerns and driveway width considered

Lower court rules in homeowners' favour

Appeals court upholds the order

A utility pole that stood in the way of two homeowners widening their driveway has remained at the centre of a dispute between neighbours in Easton, Connecticut, since 2019. The disagreement began when the homeowners sought permission to remove the pole but their neighbours refused, despite an existing agreement allowing access through the property.The dispute has now reached another turning point, with the Connecticut Appellate Court upholding an order requiring the neighbours to approve the work needed to remove the pole. The decision means the homeowners can move ahead with plans to widen their driveway, subject to the utility companies carrying out the necessary work.According to legal information website Justia , the case involved Robert J. Krasko and Francis L. O'Neill, who own one property, and Robert Konkos and Chelsea Konkos, who previously owned the neighbouring property. The appeal was decided on November 10, after the neighbours challenged a 2025 ruling in favour of the homeowners.The disagreement centred on a 25-foot-wide access route connecting the homeowners' property to a public road. Although the route was meant to provide vehicle access, an old utility pole occupied part of the space needed for their driveway.The two properties were originally part of a subdivision created in 1978.The homeowners' plot did not have direct access to the public road, so a route across the neighbouring property was provided.In December 2015, an agreement formally gave the owner of the land without direct road access the right to use this route. It allowed people to travel across it on foot or by vehicle and permitted the construction of a shared driveway.The agreement also required the neighbouring property owners not to block access through the designated area.However, a utility pole already stood close to the middle of this route. It supplied electricity and telephone services to the neighbouring house. A second pole was installed later to serve the house built on the other property, but the older one remained because it continued to carry the neighbours' electrical connection.When Krasko and O'Neill bought the property, their driveway ran close to the older pole. They wanted to widen it but said the pole made it difficult to use the available space.They approached their neighbours for permission to have it removed. The neighbours declined, leading the homeowners to file a lawsuit in, 2019.Removing the old pole was not simply a matter of taking it down. The electricity connection serving the neighbours' house also had to be transferred to the newer pole.The initial proposal involved installing new electrical cables. This would have required digging up parts of the neighbours' driveway and yard, raising concerns about expense and disruption.The homeowners later suggested a different arrangement. Under the revised plan, the existing cable would be disconnected from the old pole and extended through a seven-foot trench to the newer one. A splice box would connect the cable to the new pole.This approach meant that the neighbours would not need a completely new electrical connection. The work was expected to cause only a short interruption to their electricity supply.The homeowners asked the court to require their neighbours to approve this revised plan and allow the old pole to be removed.During the trial in November 2024, both sides presented expert assessments of the driveway and the work required to widen it.The homeowners argued that the existing driveway was too narrow for comfortable and safe access. Their engineer, James Luczak, measured its usable width at eight-and-a-half feet.He also pointed to a steep drop on the opposite side of the driveway. According to his assessment, widening the driveway in that direction would require a retaining wall about 175 feet long and seven feet high.The neighbours disputed this assessment. Their experts said the driveway was wider than the measurement provided by the homeowners' engineer. They also believed that a much smaller retaining wall could provide an alternative way to expand it.The neighbours further questioned whether removing the pole was necessary, pointing out that vehicles had managed to use the existing driveway.Krasko told the court that some delivery vehicles had struggled to pass the pole. He also raised concerns about driving through the narrow space during snowy or icy conditions.The court considered these competing accounts along with photographs, property records and expert evidence.It also examined local zoning requirements. Under Easton's regulations, driveways longer than 200 feet must be at least 12 feet wide. Both sides agreed that the driveway exceeded 200 feet and was narrower than the required width.On May 21, 2025, the trial court ruled that the homeowners could proceed with their proposed plan. It found that removing the pole would help address the driveway's width and safety problems. It also considered the alternative of widening the driveway on the opposite side impractical because of the drop in the ground and the engineering work involved.The court was not convinced that the revised electrical plan would cause significant problems for the neighbours. Evidence presented during the trial indicated that transferring the existing connection was routine work and could be completed by a licensed electrician.The expected interruption to the neighbours' electricity supply was estimated at two to three hours. The court therefore directed the neighbours to provide the necessary authorisation for the utility companies to remove the old pole and transfer their electrical connection to the newer one.The neighbours challenged this decision, arguing that the homeowners had other ways to widen their driveway and that the proposed work could affect their property.The Connecticut Appellate Court has now upheld the lower court's decision. It found that the homeowners had a valid right to use the access route and that their plan to widen the driveway was reasonable in the circumstances.The judges also noted that the availability of another option did not automatically mean the homeowners had to choose it. The alternative would involve substantial construction work because of the steep ground beside the driveway.The court also considered the changes since the original agreement was signed. At that time, the older pole was the only source of electricity for the neighbours' house. A second pole was installed later, making it possible to transfer the existing connection without the extensive work initially proposed.The neighbours had also argued that the lower court had granted a type of legal relief that the homeowners had not formally requested. The appellate court disagreed, saying the order specifically required the neighbours to approve the utility work. It was therefore an order to take action, not merely a statement about the parties' property rights.The appeals court affirmed the judgment in favour of Krasko and O'Neill. All three judges on the panel agreed with the decision.
Article Summary: The dispute centred on a 25-foot-wide access route connecting the homeowners' property to a public road. Although the route was meant to provide vehicle access, an old utility pole occupied part of the space needed for their driveway. The disagreement began when the homeowners sought permission to remove the pole but their neighbours refused, despite an existing agreement allowing access through the property.

Article Title: WWE star Titus O'Neil grew up knowing what it meant to need food assistance; his foundation has now teamed with a Tampa charity to give 500 families Thanksgiving boxes, each containing meals for four
Article Text:
Metropolitan Ministries plans to support 30,000 families through four holiday tent locations across three Florida counties.

500 families receive Thanksgiving food boxes

Childhood struggles inspire community work

Metropolitan Ministries prepares for holiday rush

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A legacy beyond the wrestling ring

For former WWE star Titus O’Neil, Thanksgiving is about more than a festive meal, a gathering of loved ones or a holiday tradition. It is a reminder of the difficult childhood days when putting food on the table was not always guaranteed and the kindness of others made all the difference. Now, years after overcoming those hardships, the Tampa philanthropist is helping ensure hundreds of local families experience a more hopeful holiday season.O’Neil, whose real name is Thaddeus Bullard, joined forces with Metropolitan Ministries through his Bullard Family Foundation to distribute 500 Thanksgiving food boxes to families in Tampa. The annual initiative took place Saturday morning outside the Thaddeus M. Bullard Academy at Sligh Middle Magnet School, a fitting location named in honor of the former professional wrestler.According to Spectrum News, more than 50 volunteers spent over three hours helping distribute the boxes, each containing enough food to feed four to six people. FOX 13 in Tampa Bay reported that the packages, known as Boxes of Hope, included proteins, side dishes and other essentials needed to prepare a traditional Thanksgiving meal.The distribution has become an annual tradition for O’Neil, who has maintained a partnership with Metropolitan Ministries for 11 years, the report stated.The initiative carries personal significance for the former WWE Tag Team Champion, who experienced food insecurity growing up. After receiving support and kindness from his community when he was struggling, he is committed to helping families.O'Neil said he uses the annual distribution to fight hunger and pay forward the help that got his family through hard Thanksgivings, according to Spectrum News and Creative Loafing Tampa Bay.The need for assistance has become increasingly pressing amid rising household expenses. As reported by FOX 13 in Tampa Bay, O’Neil pointed to escalating grocery and fuel prices as factors contributing to the growing financial pressure on families.The Thanksgiving distribution is part of a much larger effort to support vulnerable households across the Tampa Bay region.Metropolitan Ministries President and CEO Sarah Combes said the nonprofit is preparing to assist 30,000 families during the Thanksgiving and Christmas season. The initiative will operate through four holiday tent locations across Hillsborough, Pinellas and Pasco counties.According to Spectrum News, O’Neil also contributed $40,000 earlier in November toward Metropolitan Ministries' Holiday Tent initiative, further strengthening the organization's seasonal assistance programme.The nonprofit's efforts extend beyond its partnership with the Bullard Family Foundation, with 35 partner organizations and community donations helping support its holiday outreach, AOL and Men's Journal reported.O’Neil's charitable contributions have earned recognition beyond Tampa. WWE included him in its 2020 Hall of Fame class, presenting him with the Warrior Award in recognition of his humanitarian work in Tampa and internationally. His legacy includes his wrestling achievements and his latest Thanksgiving drive to help needy families.Images Courtesy: Dave Decker/Creative Loafing Tampa Bay
Article Summary: Former WWE star Titus O'Neil helped distribute 500 Thanksgiving food boxes to families in Tampa. Metropolitan Ministries plans to support 30,000 families through four holiday tent locations across three Florida counties. The initiative carries personal significance for the former WWE Tag Team Champion, who experienced food insecurity growing up.

Article Title: Florida jury awarded $6 million to the wife and two daughters of Carlos Chalbaud, who died on the operating table during elective neck surgery at Holy Cross Hospital without clearance from a cardiolog
Article Text:
Jury awarded Chalbaud's family $6 million after finding medical providers responsible for his fatal surgery complications.

Abnormal heart test, surgery anyway

Hospital and medical team held responsible

Wife and daughters receive $6 million award

A routine medical procedure intended to address a neck condition ended in tragedy for a Florida family, turning an elective surgery into a fatal medical negligence case. More than three years after 52-year-old Carlos Chalbaud suffered cardiac arrest on the operating table, a Broward County jury has held the hospital and medical professionals responsible, awarding $6 million to his wife and two daughters over failures surrounding his preoperative assessment and surgical care.The verdict followed a three-week trial, with jurors' deliberations interrupted by a two-day courthouse closure caused by severe flooding. According to the Miami Herald, the decision was delivered on Friday, following the proceedings in Broward County.According to Morning Star report, Chalbaud had elective cervical stenosis surgery at Holy Cross Hospital in Fort Lauderdale on April 3, 2023. However, his preoperative electrocardiogram (EKG) showed abnormalities, and a cardiologist declined to provide surgical clearance, recommending a comprehensive cardiac evaluation instead.CBS 12 reported that the lawsuit claimed the recommended assessment was never done.However, nurse practitioner Glenda W Thomas cleared Chalbaud for general anesthesia, saying he had no medical contraindications. The surgery subsequently proceeded despite the absence of the requested cardiology clearance.Overseeing Chalbaud during surgery was another issue during the trial. His blood pressure and heart rate reportedly declined for approximately 30 minutes before his heart stopped, the online report added.Morning Star reported that the anaesthesia record contained a gap of around 17 minutes during which no vital signs were documented, becoming a significant element of the family's negligence case.The lawsuit named Holy Cross Hospital, Thomas and members of the anaesthesia team, including physician Robert A. Drozd and certified registered nurse anaesthetist Larisa Turetsky.Following the trial, jurors assigned 30% liability to the nurse practitioner, 60% to the anaesthesiology team and the remaining 10% to the hospital.According to the Sun Sentinel, the jury determined that the failures by the medical providers contributed to Chalbaud's death, resulting in a combined $6 million award for his immediate family. The proceedings were overseen by Senior Judge Carlos Rodriguez. Jurors began deliberations on November 17, but severe flooding forced the courthouse to close for two days before they returned to deliver their decision.Chalbaud's wife, Anabella Acosta, and their daughters, Miranda and Sofia, were each awarded $2 million in damages. The jury also granted an additional $20,000 to cover medical and funeral expenses, according to Morning Star.The family's history was also presented during the proceedings. Chalbaud and Acosta married in Venezuela in 2003 before relocating to Maryland in 2018 to provide better educational opportunities for their daughters. He had built a career in the corporate sector, eventually becoming chief operating officer at Vepica, and obtained US citizenship three months before his death.The verdict brings a significant legal development for the family, whose case centred on whether medical providers should have proceeded with an elective operation despite abnormal cardiac findings and the absence of specialist clearance.Image Courtesy: Google Gemini

Article Title: Britain net migration falls to 77,000, lowest level since 1997 outside pandemic
Article Text:
Britain's net migration has fallen to its lowest level since 1997, excluding the pandemic period, as tighter immigration rules reshape migration trends/Representative Image

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Britain's annual net migration fell to 77,000 in the year to June, marking its lowest level in nearly three decades outside the COVID-19 pandemic, according to official figures released on Thursday. The decline offers some relief to the Labour government amid continued political pressure over immigration, but economists have warned that a shrinking migrant workforce could weigh on economic growth.Data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed that net migration dropped from 204,000 in the 12 months to June last year to 77,000 in the latest reporting period.The latest figure takes net migration down by around 90% from its peak in 2023, when the number of people arriving in Britain exceeded those leaving by nearly one million.The decline also brings migration closer to levels that successive governments have sought to achieve. Former Conservative Prime Minister David Cameron pledged in 2010 to bring annual net migration down to the "tens of thousands", although his government did not meet that target.Despite the sharp fall, immigration continues to feature prominently in Britain's political debate. A YouGov poll published this week found that it was the second-biggest concern among voters, behind the economy, Reuters reported.The issue has remained politically contentious for more than a decade, with both legal migration and unauthorised arrivals shaping public debate. Concerns about immigration from the European Union were among the factors that influenced the 2016 Brexit referendum.The latest reduction in net migration follows restrictions introduced by previous governments on work visas. These included limits on migrants bringing family dependents to Britain and higher salary requirements intended to prioritise skilled workers with graduate-level qualifications.The Labour government has indicated that it plans to impose further restrictions. Earlier this month, it announced proposals to double the standard qualifying period for permanent settlement from five years to 10 years, as public concern over immigration continued.Migration has played a significant role in changing Britain's population over the past 30 years. Arrivals increased following the European Union's 2004 expansion and rose again after Brexit in 2020. Net migration subsequently reached a record 944,000 in the year to March 2023, before beginning its steep decline.
Article Summary: Annual net migration fell to 77,000 in the year to June, official figures show. Figure is the lowest since 1997, excluding the COVID-19 pandemic period. The decline offers some relief to the Labour government amid political pressure. But economists have warned that a shrinking migrant workforce could weigh on economic growth.

Article Title: An Alaska pilot who grew up in a village with no roads or shops revived an old Thanksgiving tradition in her single-engine plane, dropping frozen turkeys in burlap sacks to remote families every year
Article Text:
An Alaska pilot who grew up in a village with no roads or shops revived an old Thanksgiving tradition in her single-engine plane, dropping frozen turkeys in burlap sacks to remote families every year since 2022/Image: AP

How a childhood memory inspired the Alaska Turkey Bomb

From three dozen turkeys to an annual Thanksgiving tradition

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pilot hopes to take the tradition to more Alaskan villages

For families living in remote parts of Alaska, a Thanksgiving turkey can arrive in an unusual way: falling from the sky in a burlap sack. Pilot Esther Keim has been bringing back this annual surprise since 2022, continuing a tradition started decades ago by a local aviator who once made the holiday special for her hometown.Keim flies her single-engine Stinson over isolated homes and communities, releasing frozen turkeys secured in specially prepared sacks. The deliveries, known as the ‘Alaska Turkey Bomb’, are intended to help families celebrate Thanksgiving while reminding them that they have not been forgotten.The initiative is also a tribute to Kenny Hughes, the pilot whose generosity left a lasting impression on Keim when she was growing up in Skwentna.Skwentna, where Keim spent her childhood, is a small Alaskan community without road connections, grocery stores or a conventional electricity grid. Residents depend on aircraft, riverboats and snow machines to bring in supplies, making food storage and planning particularly important during the long winter months.According to SunnySkyz, Hughes had made a habit of flying over remote homes before Thanksgiving and dropping turkeys for families.His deliveries became a much-anticipated part of the holiday for residents, including Keim, who remembers the small gestures he made for children.She recalled how Hughes would sometimes drop a newspaper containing a pack of gum. For children who could not simply walk into a shop to buy something, even that modest gift carried considerable meaning.Years later, Keim found herself in a position to bring the tradition back. By then, she had moved to Wasilla, become a private pilot and purchased her first aircraft.The idea took shape during a visit to Skwentna in spring 2022. While speaking to a local family, she heard about the difficulties they had faced getting through the winter. The father described their limited food supply with a remark that stayed with her."One squirrel doesn't split three ways very far for dinner," he told her.The conversation brought back memories of Hughes and his Thanksgiving flights. Keim realised she could use her own aircraft to offer similar help to families in the area.Keim's first delivery run took place that Thanksgiving in 2022. She distributed 36 frozen turkeys across an area covering approximately 75 miles of remote Alaska, as per the outlet.People began contributing to the initiative as news of the effort spread. Volunteers also stitched burlap sacks to carry the frozen birds, securing them with bright yellow tape to make the packages easier to identify against the snow.What began as a tribute to Hughes has since become an annual effort. Keim has continued flying the deliveries every Thanksgiving, bringing the tradition back to the communities where she grew up.For residents living off the grid, the gesture carries significance beyond the food itself. Many have limited opportunities to interact with people outside their immediate communities, and the unexpected deliveries serve as a reminder that others are thinking of them.Keim said the initiative helps recipients feel connected and supported."The people that live off the grid they don't get a lot of interaction with other people and so it just is a feeling of 'I'm not alone, someone cares enough to do this'," she said.Although Keim currently focuses on the region she knows best, she hopes the project can eventually reach more remote communities across Alaska.Keim hopes the initiative will eventually extend beyond turkey deliveries and reach more villages across Alaska, with several possibilities for expanding the effort"I'm just reaching this area because it's what I know. I would love to reach more villages. I hope it could be turned into something pretty awesome where it's just not turkeys... there's lots of possibilities," she said.
Article Summary: Esther Keim flies her single-engine Stinson over isolated homes and communities, releasing frozen turkeys secured in specially prepared sacks. The deliveries, known as the ‘Alaska Turkey Bomb’, are intended to help families celebrate Thanksgiving while reminding them they have not been forgotten.

Article Title: Congo Ebola outbreak crosses 12,000 cases as fighting disrupts response
Article Text:
The ongoing Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo has now surpassed 12,000 confirmed cases since May.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) has crossed 12,000 confirmed cases, according to government data released on Thursday.Clashes between rebel groups and the army are disrupting efforts to control the spread of the disease, reported by news agency AP.The outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic in history, with 12,021 confirmed cases and nearly half of those infected having died, data from Congo's Health Ministry showed.It is also the deadliest among the country's 17 Ebola outbreaks and could surpass the West African epidemic of 2014-2016, which claimed around 11,000 lives.Declared in May, the current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which no approved vaccine or treatment is available. Health teams are struggling to contain the disease amid armed conflict, poor road connectivity and resistance from residents driven by mistrust and misinformation.Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of infected people, including those who have died from the disease. Containment efforts require the early identification and isolation of patients, monitoring of people who may have been exposed and safe burial of victims.Fighting between the Congolese army and the convention pour la revolution populaire (CRP) rebels resumed on Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 km north of Bunia.The clashes forced more people to flee towards Bunia, the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a key centre for the Ebola response.The CRP is among more than 100 armed groups operating in eastern Congo, where prolonged conflict has fuelled a severe humanitarian crisis. The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International criminal court in 2012 for recruiting and using children under 15 in armed conflict.Earlier clashes between the army and rebels had prevented health teams from reaching some communities, disrupted the monitoring of people exposed to the virus and reduced staffing at some treatment centres, said Dr Catherine Smallwood, the world health organization's Ebola incident manager, on Wednesday.She further said, around a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday. They had been trapped for three days in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.
Article Summary: The outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic in history, with 12,021 confirmed cases and nearly half of those infected having died. It is also the deadliest among the country's 17 Ebola outbreaks and could surpass the West African epidemic of 2014-2016, which claimed around 11,000 lives.

Article Title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan seeks execution delay, says he was defending Taliban
Article Text:
File photo: Nidal Hasan, charged with killing 13 people and wounding 31 in a November 2009 shooting spree at Fort Hood

Hasan wants to revive defence barred at trial

What happened in the Fort Hood attack?

Execution controversy and survivors’ objections

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan has asked a federal court to delay his scheduled execution, saying he intends to argue that he was defending the Taliban from an unlawful US military attack.In a court filing signed by Hasan on Tuesday, he said he intended to demonstrate that the military court’s judgment and his death sentence had been obtained and were being maintained in violation of his federal constitutional and statutory rights.The filing could delay the Trump administration’s plans to execute Hasan on December 3. A hearing has been scheduled for Wednesday morning.Hasan, who is representing himself with assistance from lawyers at the American Civil Liberties Union’s Capital Punishment Project, said he intended to continue representing himself in the legal fight.One of Hasan’s central arguments is that he was prevented from presenting a defence that his actions were legally justified because he was trying to protect the Afghan Taliban from what he described as an unlawful attack by the US Army.Hasan had argued that he was acting in “defense of others”, according to court documents. However, the military judge barred him from presenting that argument during his 2013 trial.After dismissing his lawyers and choosing to represent himself, Hasan largely remained silent during the three-week trial.While the military called nearly 90 witnesses, Hasan called none in his defence and made no closing argument.A military jury found him guilty of multiple counts of murder and attempted murder for the shooting, which left 13 people dead and 32 wounded.The case has been assigned to US district judge Tony Mattivi in Kansas, where Hasan is being held at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth. Mattivi was nominated by president Donald Trump and confirmed by the Senate in June.On November 5, 2009, Hasan walked into the Soldier Readiness Processing Center at Fort Hood, Texas, where soldiers were waiting for medical tests and preparing for deployment.He opened fire with a handgun fitted with laser sights, killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others.Hasan was shot by law enforcement officers during the attack, leaving him paralysed from the waist down and confined to a wheelchair.He was convicted by a military jury in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. The jury sentenced him to death.Trump authorised Hasan’s execution on the recommendation of defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The execution, scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, would be the first US military execution by firing squad since World War II and the first military execution since 1961.The plan drew controversy after Hegseth announced that the execution would be public and the Pentagon confirmed it would be livestreamed. Critics from both parties raised concerns that broadcasting the execution could fuel radicalisation and turn it into a spectacle.Trump later said the execution would not be livestreamed, but that immediate family members of the victims could witness it in person if they chose.The latest court filing comes amid further dispute over who will be allowed to attend. Military officials have denied requests from three survivors of the 2009 shooting to witness the execution, citing regulations, security and space constraints.The survivors argued that the military should recognise them as victims under a broader definition that includes direct physical, emotional or financial harm. The Army rejected their appeal, saying regulations specify who may attend a military execution.
Article Summary: Nidal Hasan killed 13 people and wounded 31 in a November 2009 shooting spree. He was convicted by a military jury in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder. The jury sentenced him to death and he was due to be executed on December 3. Hasan has asked a federal court to delay his scheduled execution. He intends to argue he was defending the Taliban from an unlawful US military attack.

Article Title: Netanyahu's corruption trial at a turning point? Israeli judges question key charges against PM
Article Text:
File photo: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu

Three cases at the centre of trial

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Political future in the balance

Israeli judges on Wednesday urged prosecutors to reconsider three corruption cases against prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu . The judge stated that the chances of convicting him in one bribery case were low and questioned whether an offence had been committed in another, in a major setback for the long-running prosecution.The judges at the Jerusalem District Court summoned Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, who has the authority to decide whether the cases should proceed, and asked her to consider dropping one of the charges and reassessing the others.The panel said there was little likelihood of a conviction in Case 4,000, which alleges that Netanyahu granted regulatory favours to a telecommunications mogul in exchange for favourable coverage on a news website. The judges also expressed serious doubts over whether the alleged conduct in Case 2,000, involving a proposed deal with a newspaper publisher, amounted to a criminal offence.They left open the possibility of a conviction in Case 1,000, in which Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust for accepting gifts from wealthy businessmen in return for helping them with their interests.Baharav-Miara told the court that she and her team would consider the judges’ recommendations and remain open to all options based on the evidence, according to a transcript provided by a Justice Ministry spokeswoman to New York Times.The judges stressed that their remarks reflected their assessment of the evidence at this stage and did not amount to a verdict.Netanyahu, who has denied all wrongdoing and described the prosecution as a political witch hunt, said the trial had collapsed and called for it to end immediately.“Today, the trial has fallen,” he said in a televised statement, describing the judges’ comments as “a ray of truth and justice”.The prime minister said it had taken 10 years for the truth to emerge, referring to the investigations into his conduct that began about a decade ago. He also spoke of the “terrible suffering” endured by him and his family.Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate but interlocking cases. Prosecutors allege that he granted government and regulatory benefits to business figures in exchange for gifts and favourable media coverage for him and his family.In Case 4,000, Netanyahu is accused of helping the controlling shareholder of Israel’s largest telecommunications company, Bezeq, in return for positive coverage on the news website Walla, which the businessman owned. The judges said the chances of conviction in the bribery case were low enough to warrant reconsideration.Case 2,000 concerns an alleged backroom arrangement between Netanyahu and the owner of a popular daily newspaper. The proposed deal, which never came to fruition, would have involved favourable coverage of Netanyahu in exchange for measures against a rival publication. The judges said they had serious doubts that the evidence established a criminal offence.Case 1,000 involves allegations that Netanyahu accepted nearly $300,000 in gifts, including cigars and champagne, from Hollywood producer Arnon Milchan and Australian billionaire James Packer between 2007 and 2016.Prosecutors allege that Netanyahu sought to help Milchan extend a tax exemption and used his influence to assist him in renewing his US visa. The attorney general said the options in this case were either a verdict or a plea deal.Netanyahu completed his testimony in June, prompting the judges to take stock of the proceedings, which have been delayed over the years, including by the war in Gaza.The development comes at a crucial moment for Netanyahu, whose political future has been thrown into uncertainty after last month’s election failed to produce a clear parliamentary majority.His rival, former military chief and centrist Gadi Eisenkot, has been given the first opportunity by Israel’s president to form a new government. Netanyahu and his allies won more seats than Eisenkot’s bloc but fell short of securing an outright majority.Netanyahu’s indictment and trial have contributed to years of political instability in Israel, with several mainstream parties refusing to join coalitions led by him, arguing that he is unfit to govern while facing criminal charges.The judges’ intervention could now give Netanyahu a significant political boost, though the cases remain before the court and no final decision has been made on whether they will be dropped or proceed to judgment.
Article Summary: Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate but interlocking cases. Prosecutors allege that he granted government and regulatory benefits to business figures in exchange for gifts and favourable media coverage for him and his family. Netanyahu, who has denied all wrongdoing, said the trial had collapsed and called for it to end immediately.

Article Title: ‘Justice is not for sale’: California governor Newsom demands federal reforms to limit presidential pardon powers
Article Text:
Newsom targets Trump over pardons, alleges clemency has become a business under his watch

Trump hits back at Newsom

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

California governor Gavin Newsom has called for sweeping federal reforms to the US president's power to grant pardons, accusing President Donald Trump of using the Justice Department to protect wealthy allies and politically connected individuals.He alleged that clemency had become a business under the Trump administration.In a post on X, Newsom said, "No president should be able to sell a pardon. Today, I’m calling for sweeping federal reform of the presidential pardon power. The Justice Department is not Donald Trump’s personal law firm. Justice is NOT for sale."In a video message accompanying the post, Newsom criticised MAGA supremo for delivering remarks at the department of justice (DOJ) alongside Attorney General Pam Bondi, who previously served as his personal defence lawyer."Today, Donald Trump is once again standing inside the Department of Justice next to his former personal defence lawyer, who is now the Attorney General, giving a speech about protecting American families," Newsom said.Questioning Trump's record on criminal justice, Newsom referred to the 1989 case involving five Black and Latino teenagers who were wrongfully accused of raping and assaulting a woman in New York's Central Park.The teenagers, later known as the Central Park Five, were exonerated after DNA evidence and a confession by another individual established their innocence."In 1989, you took out full-page ads screaming for the death penalty for five Black and Latino teenagers before a trial, before a shred of evidence. They were innocent. DNA proved it. You never apologised," Newsom said.The California governor also defended his own clemency decisions, insisting that individuals on the state's former death row would remain behind bars for life."To the families standing with him today, your grief is real. That's why every person, every person on California's former death row will die in prison. No one walks out," he said, contrasting his approach with Trump's use of presidential pardons.Newsom alleged that several individuals convicted of serious offences had received presidential pardons after making financial contributions or benefiting from personal connections involving Trump's political circle.Citing specific cases, he alleged that a billionaire facing bribery charges had secured a pardon after his family arranged a $50 million deal involving Trump's lawyer. He also claimed that an individual convicted of stealing $10 million from nursing home workers received clemency after his mother attended a million-dollar dinner at Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.Newsom also criticised Trump's decision to pardon former Blackwater security contractors convicted in connection with the 2007 killing of 14 Iraqi civilians, including two children, in Baghdad.He further referred to the pardon of a participant in the January 6 Capitol riot who subsequently pleaded guilty to soliciting what he believed was a 15-year-old girl for sex. Newsom also criticised Trump's pardon of a foreign leader accused of facilitating large-scale cocaine trafficking into the United States."Nearly two billion, nearly $2 billion owed to victims and their families, gone. His own pardon attorney said it out loud: 'No MAGA left behind'," Newsom alleged.Accusing Trump of applying different standards of justice based on an individual's wealth and political connections, Newsom said, "Donald Trump doesn't oppose mercy. He sells it. If you're poor, Black, or Brown, you get the needle. If you're rich and know Donald Trump, you get a pardon and a personal phone call."He also raised concerns over Trump's remarks suggesting that more pardons could be forthcoming, including his statement that the possibility of pardoning himself was not unreasonable."A Justice Department that prosecutes his enemies and pardons himself and his friends? That's not law enforcement. That's a protection racket," Newsom said.Calling for structural changes to presidential clemency powers, Newsom said reforms were needed to prevent future presidents from using their constitutional authority to grant pardons for personal or financial benefit."We need foundational federal reform, starting with this: no president can ever again turn the power of mercy into a business. No president and no one should be able to sell a pardon," he said.Concluding his video message, the California governor reiterated that the Justice Department must function independently and serve the American people."A Justice Department is not Donald Trump's law firm. Justice is not for sale--not in California, and not in America," Newsom added.Newsom's remarks came after Trump sharply criticised the California Governor over his decision to grant clemency to 548 death row inmates, including individuals convicted of murdering children.Speaking at the Department of Justice on Monday (local time), Trump described Newsom's decision as one of the most shocking acts of injustice in the country. He accused the Governor and what he termed the Radical Left of prioritising convicted criminals over victims and their families."We're here today to talk about one of the most shocking acts of injustice our country has ever seen... Just days ago, the Governor of California, Gavin Newsom, granted clemency and mercy to 548 of the most EVIL monsters on the face of the Earth," Trump said.The US President also announced a Presidential Directive ordering the DOJ to seek the death penalty for individuals convicted of murdering children, as well as rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims."I will sign a Presidential Directive ordering the DOJ to seek the death penalty for child murderers, as well as rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims. My order also directs the Attorney General to expedite the execution of federal death sentences. Once juries have spoken, capital punishment will be swift and certain," Trump said.He also referred to an executive order signed on the first day of his administration, directing the DOJ to pursue capital punishment for individuals convicted of murdering law enforcement officers.Trump further announced nearly $150 million in public safety grants to support the recruitment of more than 1,000 additional sworn law enforcement officers and improve responses to domestic violence and sexual assault cases.Additionally, he backed a legislative proposal introduced by Representative Brandon Gill, titled the 'Just Punishment for Murder Act'.The proposal seeks to strengthen capital punishment provisions and expand their application to individuals convicted of murdering law enforcement officers and illegal immigrants accused of murder.
Article Summary: California governor Gavin Newsom has called for sweeping federal reforms to the US president's power to grant pardons. He accused President Donald Trump of using the Justice Department to protect wealthy allies and politically connected individuals. Newsom's remarks came after Trump sharply criticised the California Governor over his decision to grant clemency to 548 death row inmates.

A FedEx cargo aircraft overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Wednesday night, forcing the temporary closure of all but one runway and disrupting flight operations on the eve of Thanksgiving.There were no immediate reports of injuries in the incident, which occurred around 8:40 pm, the airport said. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the scene.The McDonnell Douglas MD-11 was arriving from Memphis when it ran off the runway. In that incident, an engine detached from the aircraft during takeoff, killing three pilots and 12 people on the ground.The FAA subsequently approved Boeing's proposed fix for the aircraft, and FedEx resumed operating its MD-11 fleet in May.The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said it had no information about Wednesday's incident.

Article Title: New Haven agrees to pay $30 million to George Gould, who spent nearly 27 years in prison, and the estate of Ronald Taylor, who died in 2011, after their convictions in a 1993 murder were thrown out
Article Text:
New Haven's $30 million settlement awaits committee review and Board of Alders approval for borrowing.

Two men convicted in a 1993 murder

A lengthy legal battle before exoneration

$30 million settlement and approval process

Wrongful-conviction settlements reach $77 million

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

More lawsuits remain unresolved

Nearly three decades behind bars, a conviction that unravelled years later and a settlement worth millions of dollars have brought two wrongful-conviction cases in Connecticut closer to a conclusion. The city of New Haven has agreed to pay $30 million to George Gould and the estate of Ronald Taylor, who were imprisoned for a 1993 murder they did not commit. While Gould will receive $18 million after spending almost 27 years incarcerated, Taylor's estate is set to receive $12 million following his death in 2011. The settlement, reported by the New Haven Independent and Hartford Courant, marks another major financial resolution for the city as it faces mounting lawsuits linked to wrongful convictions dating back several decades.Gould and Taylor were convicted of felony murder and other charges in connection with the July 4, 1993, killing of Eugenia Vega inside her Grand Avenue bodega in New Haven.According to the New Haven Independent, the prosecution's case relied heavily on testimony from a woman who claimed to have witnessed the crime. She later revealed that she had been arrested for prostitution and interrogated while experiencing severe heroin withdrawal.She alleged that police offered to help her obtain heroin in exchange for providing the statement they wanted. Investigators reportedly found no physical evidence linking either Gould or Taylor to the killing.Years later, two relatives reportedly approached the FBI and said Vega's son had confessed to them that he had killed his father, bringing fresh scrutiny to the convictions.The men's legal struggle involved multiple court proceedings. In 2010, a Connecticut Superior Court judge granted their habeas corpus petitions on grounds of actual innocence and ordered their release.However, the state appealed, and the Connecticut Supreme Court subsequently overturned that decision. During a second habeas proceeding, their petitions were denied, the online report adds.Gould returned to prison in 2011, while Taylor was allowed to remain at home because of his terminal cancer diagnosis. He died in October 2011, after spending more than 16 years incarcerated, New Haven Independent reported.Gould continued challenging his conviction and was released in 2021 after a judge modified his sentence. The state's Conviction Integrity Unit later reviewed the case, and prosecutors moved to vacate both convictions in 2024.The agreement was reached on November 13 in two consolidated federal civil rights cases against the city, the report added.Under the settlement, Gould will receive $18 million, while Taylor's estate, administered by Mary Murphy-Taylor, will receive $12 million. The latter payment remains subject to approval by the New Haven Probate Court.According to the Hartford Courant, the agreement also requires approval from the city's Litigation Settlement Committee. The New Haven Board of Alders must subsequently approve borrowing for the settlement.The New Haven Independent reported that Gould's legal representatives include Neufeld Scheck Brustin Hoffmann & Freudenberger, the Law Offices of Richard Emanuel and the Law Office of Attorney Michael A. Jefferson.The latest agreement represents the fourth and fifth federal civil rights lawsuits New Haven has settled within three months. Earlier settlements involved Adam Carmon for $16.5 million, Vernon Horn for $15.25 million and Marquis Jackson for $15.25 million.Together, the five settlements total $77 million. According to city officials cited by the New Haven Independent and Hartford Courant, borrowing to finance the payments could result in at least $116 million in repayments over 20 years when interest is included.Mayor Justin Elicker has acknowledged the city's responsibility to address past injustices while raising concerns about the financial burden on taxpayers. He has also called for the state to share more of the costs, noting that state authorities appealed the original decision granting Gould and Taylor relief.The mayor's office has pointed to the city's lack of insurance coverage for this type of incident in 1993 and the financial implications of settling claims decades later.The financial consequences may not end with the latest agreement. According to the New Haven Independent, lawsuits involving former Alder Troy Streater and Charles Coleman Jr. remain outstanding, alongside the separate case involving Stefon Morant, in which a jury previously awarded $38 million against the city. New Haven is appealing that verdict.For Gould, the settlement brings an end to a legal struggle that continued long after his release. For Taylor's family, the compensation comes years after his death and the eventual overturning of his conviction.The agreement represents another step in addressing wrongful convictions from New Haven's past, while leaving the city to confront the continuing legal and financial consequences.Image Courtesy: George Gould (right), with the late Ronald Taylor (center). Credit: Thomas MacMillan photo
Article Summary: The city of New Haven has agreed to pay $30 million to George Gould and the estate of Ronald Taylor, who were imprisoned for a 1993 murder they did not commit. Gould will receive $18 million after spending almost 27 years incarcerated, while Taylor's estate is set to receive $12 million following his death in 2011. The settlement marks another major financial resolution for the city as it faces mounting lawsuits linked to wrongful convictions dating back several decades.

Article Title: Mark Rothko painting bought for $115,000 in 1983 sells for $17.7 million at Sotheby's New York auction, giving collectors Theodore and Ruth Baum a return of more than 150 times
Article Text:
Image: Sotheby's

From a $115,000 purchase to a $17.7 million sale: How Theodore and Baum’s ‘Vision’ performed at the New York auction

Image: Sotheby's

Why red mattered: Rothko's 1967 canvas and the colour thread through the Baum collection

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Image: Sotheby's

Baum collection results at Sotheby's: Joan Mitchell leads while all 24 works find buyers

Artefacts from 10-24 in Vision (Image: Sotheby's)

Sotheby's New York evening totals $378.7 million as Yayoi Kusama sets a $15 million record

Mark Rothko's Untitled from 1967 has sold for $17.7 million at Sotheby's in New York, more than 150 times the $115,000 that collectors Theodore and Ruth Baum paid for the painting in 1983. The couple held the work for 43 years before it went under the hammer on 16 November, where it finished above the top of its pre-sale estimate range. Rothko painted it in the final years of his life, using fiery red and brilliant tangerine, and the Baums acquired it as their first contemporary artwork. That purchase began more than two decades of passionate collecting for the couple.According to Luxury.it, the Rothko was offered on Monday 16 November in ‘Vision: The Extraordinary Collection of Theodore and Ruth Baum,’ a 6 pm evening auction. The sale formed part of The New York Sales, held at the Breuer Building from 16 to 19 November. The painting carried a pre-sale estimate of $10 million to $15 million.Sotheby's says red is perhaps Rothko's most important colour, both symbolically and aesthetically, and that this canvas shows his command of colour in conveying the breadth of human emotion. The same colour runs through the Baum collection, from Ellsworth Kelly's Red White to Lucio Fontana's slashed red canvas Concetto spaziale, Attese, and Ed Ruscha's Dimple.The collection made $109.9 million with fees, and every one of its 24 lots sold. Joan Mitchell's Green Book of Barbara Guest was the top lot at $19.3 million, against the $65,000 the couple paid in 1986. Andy Warhol's The Scream (After Munch), from 1984, made $7.9 million. A third of the lots sold below their low estimates and a quarter above their high ones.The Baum sale was one of two evening auctions that night. Together with The Now and Contemporary Evening, which made $268.7 million, it brought in $378.7 million with fees. Luxury.it reports that Yayoi Kusama's No. 3P.B., a 1960 Infinity Nets painting, sold for $15 million, a new auction record for the artist, who died in August at 97. Roy Lichtenstein's Reflections on "Painter and Model" led the night at $24.6 million.

Rothko painted it in the final years of his life, using fiery red and brilliant tangerine. The same colour runs through the Baum collection, from Ellsworth Kelly's Red White to Lucio Fontana's slashed red canvas Concetto spaziale.

Several people were arrested after pro-Palestinian protesters clashed with Israeli supporters and New York City police during a demonstration outside a kosher deli in Brooklyn on Wednesday night.The confrontation took place outside Essen NY Deli in the Midwood neighbourhood, where Israeli brokerage firm CapitIL was hosting a real estate event. Footage circulating on social media showed groups of protesters and Israeli supporters involved in physical altercations, while demonstrators also clashed with police and tried to push through barricades.The protest was organised by the Palestine Right to Return Coalition of New York and New Jersey, also known as Pal-Awda. The group alleged that the Israeli company was hosting a land sale event featuring properties in settlements in the occupied West Bank.However, a representative of CapitIL told Jewish News Syndicate that the company was not promoting any properties in the region during its visit.Tensions escalated as demonstrators confronted officers and attempted to breach police barricades. Videos from the scene showed police struggling to contain the crowds, with several protesters being taken away in handcuffs.The New York Police Department (NYPD) confirmed that multiple arrests were made during the demonstration but did not immediately disclose the exact number of people detained or the charges they could face.More than 200 police officers were deployed to the area, Israeli media outlet Ynet reported.The NYPD's Strategic Response Group (SRG), a specialised unit that has historically handled large demonstrations and violent crowd confrontations, was also deployed during the protest.New York City Councilwoman Inna Vernikov condemned the demonstration, alleging that it turned violent and featured anti-Jewish slogans, including "Intifada" and "F the Jews". In a post on X, she said four arrests had been made and that the SRG had been called to the scene.In a subsequent post, Vernikov criticised Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plan to disband the unit, arguing that Wednesday's confrontation demonstrated why it was needed to protect Jewish-owned businesses.The deployment comes amid controversy surrounding Mamdani's campaign promise to disband the NYPD's Strategic Response Group.Although the mayor announced plans to dismantle the unit, the transition is not expected to be completed until spring 2027, ABC7 reported.City Hall has said the SRG will be replaced by a civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division and a specialised 30-member police team called the First Amendment Support Team. The latter will operate under the NYPD's Community Affairs Bureau.A separate Patrol Support Division will also be established within the NYPD's Patrol Services Bureau, with officers receiving specialised crowd-management training.The clashes also come against the backdrop of rising concerns over antisemitism in New York. According to figures cited in the report, the Anti-Defamation League recorded 860 antisemitic incidents across New York City in 2025, including 278 in Brooklyn.
Article Summary: Protest took place outside Essen NY Deli in the Midwood neighbourhood. Israeli brokerage firm CapitIL was hosting a real estate event. Article Title: 'We were told he was under no investigation': JD Vance on Nvidia CEO Huang amid China spy claims
Article Text:

US Vice President JD Vance has said federal officials assured him that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not under investigation, pushing back against concerns over reports linking Huang to a woman suspected of having connections with Chinese intelligence.Speaking to CNN's Kit Maher at a pre-Thanksgiving meal for US troops in Dayton, Ohio, on Wednesday, Vance said he had received assurances from Attorney General Todd Blanche and other government officials that there was no investigation involving Huang.“We were told that he was under no investigation,” Vance said. He added that allegations against the Nvidia chief were based on anonymous reporting rather than evidence.Vance also criticised the use of anonymous sources to make allegations that could affect someone's professional position. He said people should not lose their jobs over claims that were not supported by concrete evidence.“I talked to the attorney general. I talked to other folks as well,” Vance told CNN, referring to the assurances he had received from officials in the administration.Blanche had also dismissed questions about whether Huang had been investigated. When asked about the matter on Tuesday, the attorney general responded, “For what?”Vance's remarks follow a series of public statements from senior Trump administration officials defending Huang and rejecting suggestions that the Nvidia chief or the company had been involved in wrongdoing.President Donald Trump has also backed Huang.Nvidia's board reinstated Huang as president and chief executive officer on Monday, following his departure amid reports about his alleged extramarital affairs and claims that a woman linked to him was suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence.In its announcement, Nvidia said the board had voted unanimously to reinstate Huang after discussions and meetings with him. It said directors were satisfied with his candour and ability to lead the company.The board also said it had received input from senior US government officials and was confident that Huang's reinstatement did not pose a national security risk.“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” chairman Harvey C Jones said.Nvidia also confirmed that an independent investigation into reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort would continue. The board had formed a committee comprising independent directors and appointed external legal counsel to assist with the probe. Huang has expressed support for the investigation and committed to cooperating with it.The company has also established a separate National Security and Export Control Committee, made up entirely of independent directors, to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. It said the committee would work with legal counsel and specialist advisers.
Article Summary: US Vice President JD Vance said federal officials assured him that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not under investigation. Vance said he had received assurances from Attorney General Todd Blanche and other government officials that there was no investigation. Article Title: At 43, a former finance worker quit, sold her house and travelled Europe; she returned as a search-and-rescue ranger at Arizona’s Grand Canyon

According to the National Park Service's Behind the Scenery podcast, Emily was 43 when she recorded her episode. By then, she had built a career in finance and talent management, earned two master's degrees and completed dozens of marathons, but years earlier she had decided to leave her corporate life behind, sell her house and travel through Europe. Her journey eventually brought her to Arizona's Grand Canyon, where she found a new career as a Preventive Search and Rescue Ranger. Emily shared her story in the National Park Service'spodcast episode, We Are the Rangers (and Friends) . She told the podcast she had arrived at the North Rim in 2017, after a career in finance and talent management.Prior to joining the National Park Service, Emily was a certified public accountant and then moved into talent management and leadership development. She also obtained a master’s degree in organisational development. According to the host of the podcast, Emily had one bachelor’s degree and two master’s degrees. The reason behind Emily leaving her career path came from her difficult experience in her personal life because her mother was ill and Emily wanted to take a break from her busy schedule. As she stated, it was time to appreciate the time in her life. Emily left her job, sold her house and purchased a plane ticket to Europe to travel for around 12 months with the money that she saved before.She was planning to go back to the USA, select another city and obtain employment in the same field. When Emily returned to the US, she moved to an Airstream trailer in Tucson and worked as an accountant. After this employment opportunity finished, she received an email about a seasonal position in the Grand Canyon by the Grand Canyon Conservancy.This seasonal position entailed working at the North Rim Visitor Centre and accommodation in the form of her own recreational vehicle. The salary was modest, but Emily was happy to have the chance to live within a national park. Initially, she intended to work for just eight weeks at the end of the season. During the period, she met the interpretive rangers and worked and cycled on the trails. Being an Ironman triathlete at that point, she also ran on the trails and hiked through the canyon. This inspired her to pursue her career as a ranger. As she had no prior professional experience in outdoor conservation or trail maintenance, she volunteered as part of a trail crew the winter after this. She later worked at Yosemite National Park and spent seasons doing field operations.Emily got certified as an emergency medical technician because she wished to work in faraway places. In winter 2020-2021, Emily was offered employment as an interpreter in a place called Phantom Ranch in the Grand Canyon. The job meant a 14-mile hike down one week and back out the next. Working in this place, Emily developed an interest in emergencies as well as search and rescue calls. Later, she went through training in fighting fires and got an advanced certification as an EMT. She managed to take steps towards emergency services at the North Rim because of these certifications.At the time of the interview, Emily was a Preventive Search and Rescue Ranger. Among her responsibilities, Emily mentioned helping people on the trail, riding mountain bikes and helping with emergencies. Emily was also involved with ambulances and fire engines in the developed area.It took Emily five years of careful preparation to get into the ranger position. For her, it was hard to start over again after many years of working in the private sector, but Emily considered her ranger position to be her dream job. Her experience shows how a major career change can involve several smaller steps. For Emily, leaving finance was only the beginning. Volunteering and seasonal jobs further training helped her build a new working life at the Grand Canyon.
