Article Title: A Toronto schoolgirl picked up a stone point at Fort York in 1935 and kept it for 80 years; it was later dated to 4,000-6,000 years ago
Article Text:
AI Representation: A Toronto schoolgirl picked up a stone point at Fort York in 1935 and kept it for 80 years. Image credits: Chatgpt

A small discovery during a school trip

A tool in the Archaic period

One of only four projectiles

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Fort York where a ten-year-old Jeanne Carter found an unusual souvenir. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

According to the Friends of Fort York newsletter, a school trip to Fort York in Toronto in 1935 gave ten-year-old Jeanne Carter an unusual souvenir. While walking along a sandy path towards a building, she noticed a small white stone on the ground and picked it up. She had no idea how old it was or why it might be important. Carter kept the artefact in her curio cabinet for about eighty years until a historian analysed it and found it had been made 4,000 to 6,000 years ago. The artefact was a quartzite projectile point, which dated back to the Archaic period in the Indigenous history of that place. It provided insight into the history of the area many years prior to the establishment of Fort York as a military installation.The stone was found by Carter at the Fort York field trip in 1935. In one of her recollections, Carter remembered approaching a building on a sandy track where she saw a white piece. She picked it up and took it back home. It spent nearly eight decades in her curio cabinet before it was given by Carter to her friend working in the museum. This friend then handed it over to Richard Gerrard, a historian in the City of Toronto who identified the archaeological value of the item.According to the Friends of Fort York , the stone was made from quartzite. Gerrard considered the material unusual for this part of Ontario, raising the possibility that it had travelled a considerable distance through trade or movement between communities.This item was estimated to be 4,000 to 6,000 years old; hence, it belonged to the Archaic period, a broad period of Indigenous history prior to the arrival of Europeans. Projectile points were part of Indigenous technologies and as Ontario Parks notes, were often used for hunting or butchering, yet no clear application of Carter's artefact had been defined. Neither the identity of its original owner nor the circumstances behind how it ended up at Fort York had been determined. The fact that it was made of quartzite was especially intriguing. Gerrard proposed that the arrival of this material in Toronto could indicate long-distance migration or trade. No information was provided about the origin of the rock used for creating this artefact.What made Carter's discovery unique was that it was one of just four projectile points ever found at Fort York, according to the Friends of Fort York newsletter. The other three were uncovered during excavations conducted by archaeologists. Carter, in turn, made her discovery while walking through the site during her field trip.Moreover, the artefact proved to be one of the oldest items in the City of Toronto's collection, according to the Friends of Fort York newsletter, which demonstrated that there was a lot of history hidden under the current urban environment. It was generally known that Fort York was strongly connected with Toronto's military history, namely with the War of 1812.The findings showed that people used the area for thousands of years before the fort was built. According to Wayne Reeves, who is the chief curator of Museums and Heritage Services, the archaeological material demonstrated the presence of First Nations over thousands of years. This kind of item is important historical proof because the Archaic period predates written records in the region, so archaeological finds are essential to knowing the story of the people who lived there. Having been in the possession of Carter for almost 80 years, the point was finally donated and the Friends of Fort York newsletter describes it as one of the oldest artefacts in the City of Toronto's collection.
Article Summary: A school trip to Fort York in Toronto in 1935 gave ten-year-old Jeanne Carter an unusual souvenir. Carter kept the artefact in her curio cabinet for about eighty years until a historian analysed it and found it had been made 4,000 to 6,000 years ago. The artefact was a quartzite projectile point, which dated back to the Archaic period in the Indigenous history of that place.

Article Title: A New Jersey railway bridge that entered service in 1910 had to swing open every time large boats needed to pass; 116 years later, a $2.3 billion replacement lets ships and trains pass without the bri
Article Text:
A 1910 New Jersey bridge had to open for ships; its $2.3bn replacement lets trains run uninterrupted (International Construction Equipment)

Why the original Portal Bridge had to open for boats

How the $2.3 billion replacement works

Both tracks are now in full service

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

For more than a century, a railway bridge in New Jersey had an unusual problem: whenever boats needed to travel along the river below, the entire bridge had to swing open, interrupting train services. Having entered service in 1910, the ageing structure became a recurring source of delays for commuters travelling between New Jersey and New York. Now, after years of construction, a $2.3 billion replacement has entered full service, allowing trains and marine traffic to move independently.According to an announcement by Amtrak and NJ TRANSIT on November 16, 2026, both tracks of the new Portal North Bridge are now operational. The fixed-span structure replaces the 116-year-old Portal Bridge over the Hackensack River in Kearny, New Jersey. Its elevated design allows boats to pass underneath without requiring trains to stop for a bridge opening, addressing a longstanding problem along one of the busiest passenger railway corridors in the United States.The original Portal Bridge was built by the Pennsylvania Railroad and entered service in 1910.It formed an important part of the Northeast Corridor, connecting railway routes between Newark, New Jersey, and New York. Unlike a conventional fixed railway bridge, the Portal Bridge was designed as a movable swing-span structure. It could rotate to create an opening for marine traffic travelling along the Hackensack River. Once the vessels had passed, the bridge had to return to its railway position before trains could resume crossing.Although this arrangement allowed both trains and boats to use the waterway, it created operational difficulties as railway traffic increased over the decades. The ageing bridge also developed mechanical problems and could sometimes fail to close properly after opening. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, more than 450 NJ TRANSIT and Amtrak trains carrying approximately 200,000 passengers crossed the bridge each weekday. A delay caused by a bridge opening or mechanical malfunction could therefore affect a large number of commuters and disrupt services across the wider Northeast Corridor.The new Portal North Bridge was designed to eliminate the need for a movable railway span. Instead of swinging open, it remains permanently in position, with enough clearance for marine vessels to pass beneath it. The new two-track structure rises approximately 50 feet above the Hackensack River, doubling the height clearance available under the original bridge. This allows boats to travel along the river without interrupting railway operations.The replacement project extends approximately 2.44 miles along the Northeast Corridor, including the bridge and its approaches. It also involved constructing retaining walls, concrete piers, deep foundations, steel spans and supporting railway infrastructure. The total project cost is approximately $2.36 billion, funded through federal, state and regional contributions, including investments from the US Department of Transportation, New Jersey and Amtrak. A $1.56 billion construction contract was awarded to the Skanska/Traylor Bros joint venture in October 2021.The project is part of the broader Gateway Program, which aims to modernise and expand passenger railway infrastructure between Newark and New York.The transition from the original bridge to the replacement took place in stages to maintain railway operations during construction. The first track of the new Portal North Bridge entered service on March 15, 2026, while the old swing bridge continued operating for trains using the second track. The final transfer began on October 9 and was completed on November 16, when both tracks became fully operational.The transition involved five weeks of railway service adjustments, including diversions affecting some NJ TRANSIT commuters travelling towards New York. With the second track now operational, regular service has resumed and the temporary diversions have ended. The new bridge is expected to reduce delays, improve reliability and allow trains to operate more efficiently.It also supports higher train speeds, with the new crossing designed for speeds of up to 90 miles per hour, compared with 60 miles per hour on the original bridge.The 1910 Portal Bridge is scheduled to be dismantled in 2027. Its replacement marks the end of a century-long arrangement in which railway services had to make way for passing vessels. For commuters and river traffic alike, the new crossing represents a significant change: trains can continue moving while boats pass underneath, without either having to wait for the bridge to open or close.
Article Summary: The new Portal North Bridge replaces the 116-year-old Portal Bridge over the Hackensack River in Kearny, New Jersey. Both tracks of the new bridge are now operational. Its elevated design allows boats to pass underneath without requiring trains to stop for a bridge opening.

Article Title: An Ohio family says its newly built luxury home arrived months late with about 40 defects, prompting $37,275 to be held in escrow; November 25 appeals judges revived their claims against the builder
Article Text:
Ohio family wins appeal over luxury home defects and delayed constructionAI generated representative image using Canva

What the family alleges

Why the case was revived

Leaks and claimed losses

What happens next

The broader takeaway

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

An Ohio family’s dispute over a newly built luxury home has been revived by the state’s First District Court of Appeals, giving them another chance to pursue claims against the builder. According to the appellate opinion, the DeLaets allege that Sterling Homes delayed construction for several months and delivered a home with roughly 40 defects identified during a final walkthrough. Rather than delay closing, the parties agreed to hold $37,275 in escrow while the builder addressed more significant structural problems. On November 25, the appeals court reversed a trial court’s partial summary judgment for Sterling Homes and sent the case back for further proceedings, as per details on Justia U.S. Law.The ruling does not decide whether the builder was negligent, whether the repairs were completed, or how much money the family may ultimately recover. Instead, it restores the family’s opportunity to develop and present evidence supporting their allegations. The court found that Sterling Homes had not met its initial burden when it sought summary judgment, because it did not provide adequate record evidence to show that the family could not prove financial damages.Read more details about it here:The case, Sarasota Beach House Trust v. Sterling Homes, L.L.C., was filed in January 2023 by the Sarasota Beach House Trust and trustees Edward L. DeLaet, Rebecca Kravitz DeLaet, and David DeLaet. Their complaint says Sterling Homes was responsible for constructing their new luxury home and that the project was delayed for several months before delivery. During a final walkthrough with Sterling’s property manager, the family says they identified approximately 40 items requiring repair.Rather than postpone the closing, the parties entered into an escrow arrangement involving $37,275. The stated purpose was to ensure that money would be available while Sterling addressed the more significant structural problems in the home. The DeLaets allege that, when they filed their lawsuit, many necessary repairs still had not been made.Their complaint raised four claims: breach of the construction contract, breach of the escrow agreement, violation of Ohio’s Home Construction Service Suppliers Act, and violation of the Consumer Sales Practices Act. They sought monetary damages and attorney fees. Sterling Homes denied the allegations in part and filed counterclaims alleging that it had substantially completed the repairs covered by the escrow agreement.The appeal centered on a procedural question: could Sterling obtain partial summary judgment simply by arguing that the DeLaets had no evidence of financial damage? The appellate court said no. Under Ohio’s civil rules, the party seeking summary judgment must first identify record evidence showing that no genuine dispute exists on an essential element of the claim. A bare assertion that the other side lacks proof is not enough.Sterling argued that the DeLaets had failed to respond to discovery requests and therefore could not prove damages. But the appeals court found that Sterling had not submitted affidavits, transcripts, pleadings, admissions, or other qualifying evidence to establish that claim. The only document Sterling submitted was an unauthenticated blank copy of its discovery requests, which the court said did not meet the evidentiary standard for summary judgment.The court also rejected the idea that an alleged failure to respond to discovery, by itself, proved that the DeLaets suffered no damages. Even if the family had been late in responding, the court said, that would show dilatory communication, not the absence of financial harm. The court further noted that discovery sanctions generally require a court order compelling discovery, and no such order had been issued in this case.The DeLaets described two significant leaks at the home during the summer of 2024. In affidavits, they attributed one leak to improper bathroom tiling and another to incorrectly sealed pipes inside a wall. They also stated that their financial damages exceeded $40,000, although the appellate court observed that the affidavits contained only a conclusory statement on that point.Later, in seeking reconsideration of the trial court’s ruling, the family submitted repair estimates and invoices intended to document the amount of their claimed losses. Sterling argued that those materials were created and disclosed after the discovery deadline and asked the trial court to strike them. The trial court denied both Sterling’s motion to strike and the family’s request for reconsideration.Those damages documents were not the basis of the appellate court’s decision. The appeals court reversed the earlier ruling because Sterling had failed to carry its initial evidentiary burden, not because it found the invoices or estimates sufficient to prove the family’s case. The family will still need to prove its damages and the other elements of its claims as the case moves forward.The appellate court reversed the trial court’s judgment and remanded the case to the Hamilton County Court of Common Pleas for further proceedings. That means the DeLaets’ claims are once again live, and the parties can continue discovery, address evidentiary issues, and potentially proceed toward trial if the dispute is not resolved earlier. The court made clear that the trial judge may manage evidence and party conduct under Ohio’s civil rules on remand.The decision also acknowledges concerns about the family’s litigation conduct. The appellate panel noted that the DeLaets sought a discovery extension after the deadline had passed, submitted summary judgment responses that did not directly address damages, and waited until reconsideration to present invoices and estimates. The court said those actions do not limit the trial court’s authority to impose appropriate case-management measures.For homeowners, the case is a reminder that construction disputes often turn on documentation. Walkthrough lists, photographs, contractor communications, repair invoices, expert reports, and a clearly written escrow agreement can all matter when parties disagree about whether work was completed properly. For builders, the ruling underscores that a summary judgment motion requires more than an argument that the opposing party has not yet produced proof.The appellate ruling is significant because it reinforces a basic protection in civil litigation: a defendant cannot avoid a claim merely by saying the plaintiff has no evidence. The moving party must point to admissible record evidence and show why summary judgment is warranted.In this dispute, the court concluded that Sterling had not done so.That does not guarantee a win for the DeLaets. It simply means their allegations, including the claimed construction delays, the roughly 40 walkthrough defects, and the $37,275 escrow arrangement, will receive further consideration in the trial court. The ultimate question of whether Sterling breached its obligations, completed the required repairs, or caused compensable damage remains open.
Article Summary: An Ohio family’s dispute over a newly built luxury home has been revived. The DeLaets allege that Sterling Homes delayed construction for several months and delivered a home with roughly 40 defects. Rather than delay closing, the parties agreed to hold $37,275 in escrow while the builder addressed more significant structural problems.

Article Title: A man bought a Washington property and registered it in sister's name to shield it from his wife; years later, after he developed Alzheimer's, his children challenged their aunt's ownership in court
Article Text:
Man put Washington property in sister's name to shield it from wife

Brother managed the property for nearly two decades

Alzheimer's diagnosis brought the ownership dispute into focus

Lower court recognised brother as the property's owner

Appeals court overturns adverse possession ruling

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Ownership dispute returns to lower court

A family property arrangement made nearly three decades ago has turned into a legal battle between a brother's children and their aunt in Washington, DC. In 1999, Sahr L. Bockai Sr. purchased a property in the city's Anacostia neighbourhood but had it registered in his sister Janet Finda Ahmadu's name. He reportedly wanted to protect the asset from his estranged wife amid marital difficulties. Bockai paid the deposit, repaid the mortgage and managed the property for years, while Ahmadu maintained that it had been given to her as a gift. The dispute escalated after Bockai developed Alzheimer's disease, prompting his children to challenge their aunt's ownership in court.Bockai purchased the property at 1932 Martin Luther King Jr Avenue Southeast in 1999, intending to open a pharmacy. He paid a $20,000 deposit, while a mortgage of $180,000 was taken out to finance the purchase. The deed, however, was registered in Ahmadu's name, with the mortgage arranged using her power of attorney.According to testimony from Bockai's former accountant, he had chosen this arrangement because he was separated from his wife and wanted to prevent her from claiming the property during a potential divorce.He intended to have the property transferred into his own name later for a nominal amount.Ahmadu disputed this account. She said her brother had gifted her the property in gratitude for supporting him after he immigrated to the US and while he was qualifying to work as a pharmacist.Although Ahmadu was named on the deed, Bockai handled the property's day-to-day affairs. He operated a pharmacy there, paid the mortgage, taxes and other expenses, arranged improvements and collected rent from tenants.Ahmadu said she had allowed him to manage the property because she was not in a position to do so herself. She also gave him power of attorney and did not charge him rent for using the premises. According to her account, he could use the property's proceeds for improvements and send any remaining money to her to support relatives in Sierra Leone.The siblings apparently had no significant disagreements over the arrangement for years. Their relationship with regard to the property came under strain only towards the end of the 2010s.Bockai developed Alzheimer's disease in the late 2010s. His children were subsequently appointed as his guardians following proceedings in Maryland.The children then challenged Ahmadu's ownership, arguing that their father had been the actual owner and that she was taking advantage of his deteriorating mental condition. They maintained that he had paid for and controlled the property, despite the deed being in his sister's name.During the proceedings, evidence was also presented about Bockai's use of relatives' names in other property transactions. In one instance, he had purchased a property in his son's name without initially informing him. After discovering the arrangement, the son transferred the property to his father without receiving payment. Bockai had also used his daughter's name for another property, which she regarded as belonging to him.After a three-day trial, a Washington, DC, Superior Court ruled in Bockai's favour. It concluded that he had acquired ownership through adverse possession, a legal principle under which someone may obtain rights over property after possessing it openly and continuously for a specified period.The court declared Bockai the sole legal and equitable owner of the property. It also ordered Ahmadu to reimburse him for legal costs and expenses.Ahmadu challenged the decision, arguing that her brother's management of the property had taken place with her permission and could not establish adverse possession.On September 3, 2026, the District of Columbia Court of Appeals overturned the lower court's adverse possession finding and set aside the order requiring Ahmadu to pay legal fees.Under Washington, DC, law, adverse possession requires someone to demonstrate actual, open, notorious, exclusive, continuous and hostile possession of a property for at least 15 years.The appeals court found that Bockai's management of the property had been authorised by Ahmadu through the power of attorney. She had not revoked that authority, and there was no evidence that he had told her he rejected her ownership.The court therefore concluded that his possession had not been established as hostile.The judges also noted that the siblings' relationship had apparently remained peaceful for years, with disagreements emerging only later.The appeals court's decision did not establish Ahmadu as the property's rightful owner. Instead, it sent the case back to the lower court to consider other possible legal claims.These include whether Bockai could seek compensation for the money he invested in the property, including the initial deposit and mortgage repayments. The court also left open the possibility of considering claims such as unjust enrichment or a constructive trust.The case will therefore return to the lower court, where the competing claims over the property and the financial contributions made by Bockai will be examined further.
Article Summary: Sahr L. Bockai Sr. purchased a property in Washington, DC, in 1999. He had it registered in his sister Janet Finda Ahmadu's name. He wanted to protect the asset from his estranged wife amid marital difficulties. He paid the deposit, repaid the mortgage and managed the property for years. Ahmadu maintained that it had been given to her as a gift. The dispute escalated after he developed Alzheimer's disease.

Article Title: In 1990, Sue Hendrickson discovered a T. rex in South Dakota; seven years later, its skeleton sold at auction for $8.36 million
Article Text:
Sue, the most complete T. rex skeleton ever found, on display at the Field Museum in Chicago. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

A lucky find in South Dakota

Why Sue is such a big deal

Sue Hendrickson, who spotted the first bones of Sue the T. rex in 1990, reading to children about fossils and dinosaurs in 2001. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

The fight over who owned Sue

A record-breaking auction

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What Sue is still teaching scientists

In August 1990, fossil hunter Sue Hendrickson noticed a few large bones sticking out of an eroded bluff in South Dakota. According to the Field Museum in Chicago, she followed a hunch that more was hidden under the surface. She was correct. Seven years later, the skeleton she discovered sold at auction for $8.36 million. The story is about science, money, and one big question: who owns a dinosaur?Hendrickson was on a commercial excavation trip north of the town of Faith when she stumbled upon the skeleton. The museum reports it took six people 17 days to excavate the bones. The dinosaur was named Sue after its finder, but it wasn't clear if the animal was male or female. The fossils date back to the Cretaceous era, about 67 million years ago. Growth rings in the bones, similar to those of tree rings, indicate that the dinosaur lived for about 28 years, which is at the upper end of a T. rex's life expectancy. Scientists also observed a teenage growth spurt, with the animal reaching full size at 19.Sue is the largest T. rex skeleton ever found, measuring over 40 feet (12 metres) long and 13 feet (about 4 metres) tall at the hip. It is also the most complete. About 90% of the skeleton by bone volume survived. That means that scientists have 250 of the roughly 380 bones in a T. rex skeleton, including the wishbone. The Field Museum calls Sue the most celebrated T. rex and one of the most famous fossils in the world.Peter Makovicky, the then museum's curator of palaeontology, said some questions about T. rex can only be answered by Sue. Scientists have learned about movement, intelligence, and even body weight from the bones.Finding Sue was one thing; deciding who owned it was another. Three parties began a five-year struggle for custody after the find that ended in an auction in 1997. A 2020 article published by Elizabeth D. Jones in History and Philosophy of the Life Sciences analyses the legal battles in the 1990s. Jones notes that, according to her research, academic palaeontologists, fossil collectors, Native Americans, private citizens, and government officials all claimed ownership of Sue. She argues that the debates were started and kept going by assumptions of ownership, expertise, or both.The public auction took place in 1997. The Field Museum won, with support from McDonald’s Corporation, Walt Disney World Resort, and private donors. The final price came to about $8.4 million, or $8.36 million to be exact. That was the most money ever paid for a fossil at an auction at the time.Following the sale, 12 museum preparators spent more than 30,000 hours preparing the skeleton and another 20,000 hours building the exhibit. The dinosaur was unveiled in the museum's Stanley Field Hall on 17 May 2000. The skeleton is now on display in the Evolving Planet gallery.Sue’s work is far from over. In 2016, one of the small forelimbs was scanned at the Argonne National Laboratory in Lemont, Illinois. Micro-CT scans revealed detailed images of the bone’s interior, helping scientists understand how T. rex used its arms. The actual skull, weighing 600 pounds (about 272 kilograms), is kept separately in a case for visiting scientists to study. Some scientists thought that the holes in the lower jaw were bite marks. However, it is now more commonly believed that they were the result of an infection. The museum adds that it cannot wait to find out what discoveries the skeleton will lead to next.
Article Summary: Sue is the largest T. rex skeleton ever found, measuring over 40 feet (12 metres) long and 13 feet (about 4 metres) tall at the hip. About 90% of the skeleton by bone volume survived. Scientists have learned about movement, intelligence, and even body weight from the bones.

Article Title: In 1988, hail and heavy rain knocked out both engines of a TACA Boeing at 16,000 feet; its pilots made a powerless landing on a levee near New Orleans
Article Text:
Hail rattled the nose and wings as the jet descended through the storm, minutes before an emergency landing (representative image). Image Credits: ChatGPT

A routine descent turned dangerous

The storm's hail left visible damage on the radome, the nose cover that protects the jet's weather radar. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

Failed restarts and a landing on a levee

Why did the engines shut down?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

How the lesson changed jet engines

Rain streaking across a plane window rarely worries anyone. Passengers just expect the engines to keep running no matter what the sky throws at them. That expectation failed over Louisiana on 24 May 1988. The Federal Aviation Administration's lessons learned page on TACA Flight 110 tells the story of a Boeing 737-300 that lost power in both engines while descending towards New Orleans. The agency said none of the 38 passengers and seven crew members were injured. So how did a jet with no engine power land safely, and what did the scare teach the aviation industry?The flight began in San Salvador, El Salvador, stopped in Belize City and continued towards New Orleans. The flight went normally until the descent from 35,000 feet. The FAA said the crew tried to avoid the worst storm cells but still found itself flying briefly in very heavy precipitation. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) added in its Brief of Incident that, according to the readings of weather radar, some red cells on either side of the route were spotted, and the crew decided to take a path between two of those. The FAA's account placed the power loss at roughly 16,000 feet after the jet ran into around 30 seconds of heavy hail. Both engines lost power, and the flight crew declared an emergency at 12,000 feet and radioed air traffic control (ATC).First, the pilots tried to restart both engines using the air rushing past the plane. But that did not work. Then they started the auxiliary power unit, a small onboard power source, and tried again with starter help.The engines lit up but would not speed up to idle because water and hail were still passing through them. According to the FAA, this attempt pushed engine temperatures beyond safe limits and melted turbine parts. The pilots reduced the throttle and then shut down both engines after seeing no response from the throttle. They realised the airport was too far away and started preparing to ditch. They burst through the cloud layer and saw a small levee. The FAA called the result a successful dead-stick landing, meaning the jet landed without power on a levee near New Orleans. The NTSB brief listed the damage to the aircraft as minor.According to the NTSB, the probable cause of the accident is double-engine flameout due to water ingestion following exposure to heavy rain and hail. The FAA believed that the storm was as powerful as rainfall of 30 inches, or approximately 76 centimetres per hour. However, hail worked better than rain in terms of getting through the engine core. Hail acts more like a bullet and therefore does not curve according to the direction of airflow. It can pass through the fan blades right into the core. When the core holds too much water, the fuel can no longer burn, and the flame goes out. Up until this incident, it was believed in the industry that hail and water would behave similarly within an engine.The NTSB cited inadequate engine design and the FAA’s certification standards for water ingestion as contributing causes. After some testing, CFM International (CFMI), the engine maker, changed the shape of the spinner, added a cutback splitter and more bleed valve doors, all to keep hail and water out of the core. The FAA made these changes mandatory, ordering new flight manual procedures for the 737. In 1998, the FAA issued a tougher rain and hail standard for engines, 14 CFR § 33.78. The FAA also noted the engine had four times the safety margin needed in certification tests, but the method of testing was later found to be flawed. The lesson here is pretty simple: old assumptions must be tested against new designs.
Article Summary: A Boeing 737-300 lost power in both engines while descending towards New Orleans. The pilots tried to restart both engines using the air rushing past the plane. They realised the airport was too far away and started preparing to ditch. They burst through the cloud layer and saw a small levee. The FAA called the result a successful dead-stick landing.

Article Title: JeM commander acknowledges terror network in Rawalakot
Article Text:
With the Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed increasingly coming under scrutiny for operating proxy terror outfits in Jammu and Kashmir, their focus has shifted towards reviving dormant militant groups in the Valley and using them to further their activities.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In a significant admission exposing the nexus between terror outfits and Pakistani establishment, Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) commander Masood Ilyas Kashmiri has publicly acknowledged the presence of his group’s armed terrorist network in Rawalakot in POK while alleging state authorities plan to target leaders of an ongoing regional protest movement.Addressing a gathering in Islamabad, Ilyas also criticised Pakistan’s security and intelligence agencies, questioning their failure to identify individuals allegedly involved in anti-state activities as well as those accused of killing paramilitary Pakistan Rangers personnel during recent clashes.The JeM commander went on to say that some of his group’s armed cadres belong to the same local communities that are participating in demonstrations being organised by Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a civil society coalition that has led prolonged protests over economic grievances and governance in the region.He said he had also met with Pakistani govt and security officials in Islamabad to clarify JeM’s position on the unrest. During his address, he alleged officials in Pakistan’s leadership had decided to eliminate both the leaders of the action committee and chief demonstrators in Rawalakot.Ilyas previously drew attention in Sept 2025 when he was seen in a video addressing a gathering in Balakot and acknowledging significant losses suffered by JeM during Indian military strikes on May 7 that year under Operation Sindoor.More than 150 people have died in the protests against Pakistani govt in Rawalakot in the last few months. Ilyas’s statement has brought govt’s role in the open.Amid turmoil and rising casualties of peaceful protesters in Rawalkot and neighbouring regions of POK, JAAC had recently written to Field Marshal Asim Munir, demanding an immediate end to military operations.The committee had emphasised that continued state violence will only widen the rift between the Pakistani military establishment and the local population, risking the transformation of a peaceful and democratic movement into a violent uprising.
Article Summary: Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) commander Masood Ilyas Kashmiri has publicly acknowledged the presence of his group’s armed terrorist network in Rawalakot in POK. He alleges state authorities plan to target leaders of an ongoing regional protest movement. Ilyas previously drew attention in Sept 2025 when he was seen in a video addressing a gathering in Balakot.

Article Title: Why thousands are protesting in Karachi against Asim Munir's proposal to divide Sindh
Article Text:
Sindhi nationalist groups rally in Karachi, opposing alleged plans to divide Sindh and accusing Asim Munir of undermining the province's unity (Image credit: Ayaz Latif Palijo's X)

Why Sindhi nationalist groups are opposing proposed division

Resource exploitation, land takeover allegations

JSMM announces economic blockade, Sindhudesh campaign

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Thousands of people, including political leaders and activists from various Sindhi nationalist organisations, rallied in Karachi on Monday to oppose alleged moves to divide Sindh into new administrative units.The demonstration, organised by the Jeay Sindh Rahbar Committee, accused Pakistan's Army Chief Asim Munir and Punjab of attempting to weaken Sindh's territorial unity, while raising concerns over alleged economic exploitation and control of the province's resources.The rally brought together several nationalist groups from different parts of Sindh, with opposition to the proposed administrative changes emerging as the central theme of the demonstration.According to a press release issued by the organisers, the rally was led by prominent nationalist leaders, including Riaz Chandio, Dr Niaz Kalani, Aslam Khairpuri and Nawaz Khan Zaunr, along with other senior political figures, ANI reported.Organisations participating in the demonstration included Jeay Sindh Qaumi Mahaz (Bashir Khan), Jeay Sindh Qaumi Mahaz (Aresar), Jeay Sindh Qaumparast Party and Jeay Sindh Qaumi Mahaz (Niaz Kalani).Activists of Jeay Sindh Muttahida Mahaz (JSMM), which is not formally part of the Jeay Sindh Rahbar Committee, also joined the rally.The organisers accused Punjab and Pakistan's army Chief Asim Munir of pursuing attempts to weaken Sindh's historical, territorial and national unity through the creation of new administrative units. They alleged that the proposed changes were a pretext to fragment the province.Participants declared that they would not accept any division of Sindh and insisted that its historical and geographical unity must be protected.The organisers described Pakistan as an artificial theocratic state and alleged that Sindh had faced political subordination and economic exploitation since its incorporation into the country. They asserted that the Sindhi nation had historically existed as an ancient and sovereign community.The rally also highlighted allegations of exploitation of Sindh's natural resources and agricultural land. According to the organisers, millions of acres of ancestral agricultural land, coastal islands and reserves of oil, natural gas and coal had been taken over by Punjab and the Pakistani state apparatus.The demonstration was organised to register opposition to what the groups described as internal colonial control of Sindh and to mobilise support against any proposed administrative division of the province.In a separate announcement, the central body of Jeay Sindh Muttahida Mahaz (JSMM) said it would intensify its political struggle by launching an economic blockade targeting Punjab.According to the press release, the decision was taken during a meeting of the organisation's central leadership a day before the Karachi rally. JSMM announced plans to enforce a shutdown of highways and transit routes to disrupt supply lines to Punjab.The organisation also said its movement, initially focused on defending Sindh's territorial integrity, would be expanded into a campaign demanding the complete national independence of Sindhudesh.The press release said JSMM planned to mobilise the Sindhi population, particularly young people, for sustained political mobilisation and resistance towards achieving independence from what it described as Punjabi colonial occupation.
Article Summary: Sindhi nationalist groups rally in Karachi, opposing alleged plans to divide Sindh. Accuse Pakistan's Army Chief Asim Munir of undermining the province's unity. Thousands of people, including political leaders and activists from various Sindhi nationalist organisations, rally.

Article Title: LeT, JeM proxies exposed, ISI eyes revival of 19 dormant terror outfits in Jammu and Kashmir
Article Text:
How ISI plans to rebuild terror networks in J&K

19 dormant terror outfits on ISI radar

Local recruitment, infiltration among key concerns

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence ( ISI ) is exploring a shift in its strategy in Jammu and Kashmir , with plans to bring back dormant terror outfits in the Valley as its existing proxy groups face increased scrutiny from the security agencies, news agency IANS reported.Pakistan's ugly motive is to create a network of revived terror outfits that can operate without any apparent links to established Pakistan-based organisations such as the Lashkar-e-Taiba ( LeT ) and Jaish-e-Mohammed ( JeM ), according to officials cited by IANS.The Hafiz Saeed-led LeT has been operating through The Resistance Front (TRF), while Masood Azhar's JeM has been linked to proxy outfits such as the People's Anti-Fascist Front (PAFF), Kashmir Tigers (KT) and Lashkar-e-Mustafa.However, investigations by agencies such as the Jammu and Kashmir Police and the National Investigation Agency (NIA) have increasingly exposed the links between these outfits and their parent organisations. The agencies have gathered evidence indicating that the different names are being used to mask the involvement of the LeT and JeM.An official told IANS that the ISI has now advised these groups to reconnect with former members of terror organisations that have been inactive in Jammu and Kashmir for years.Several of these outfits emerged during the 1990s and early 2000s, when militancy was at its peak in the Valley. However, as the ISI concentrated its operations around the LeT, JeM and Hizbul Mujahideen, many smaller groups gradually became inactive.Some ran out of funds, while others lost their operatives to security force operations, the official said.According to data cited by IANS, Jammu and Kashmir currently has 10 active terror groups, while 19 outfits remain inactive. Among the dormant organisations are the Kashmir Jehad Force (KJF) and Tehrik-e-Jihad (TeJ).An Intelligence Bureau official said the ISI is likely to focus on locating former members of these groups and encouraging them to rebuild their networks."These members would be told to look out for potential recruits and then revive these terror groups. There would be no direct link between these groups and the existing terror outfits. This helps the ISI in covering its tracks when an investigation into a terror attack is launched," the official said.A major consideration behind the proposed strategy is that several of these organisations are homegrown rather than Pakistan-based. Their revival could make it more difficult for investigators to establish direct links with established terror outfits operating from across the border, the report said.The ISI is also expected to draw on the experience of former members in areas such as recruitment and logistics. Although many of them are now older, officials believe their knowledge of local networks could prove useful in rebuilding the outfits.The agency is likely to focus on recruiting local youth, while Pakistan continues to explore ways to increase infiltration into Jammu and Kashmir through multiple routes, an official told IANS.Another official said the ISI is keen to restore militant activity in the Valley. However, the recent killing of Lashkar commander Lateef Bhat has dealt a setback to its plans and could delay efforts to revive terror networks for some time.The revived groups could be used for both ground operations and information warfare, including disinformation and propaganda campaigns, officials said.This would require security agencies to tackle not only possible terror operations but also coordinated attempts to influence public opinion through propaganda, adding to the security challenges in Jammu and Kashmir, the report said.
Article Summary: Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence ( ISI ) is exploring a shift in its strategy in Jammu and Kashmir. It plans to bring back dormant terror outfits in the Valley as its existing proxy groups face increased scrutiny. The revived groups could be used for both ground operations and information warfare, including disinformation and propaganda campaigns.

Article Title: Pakistan petrol pumps threaten nationwide shutdown, give govt 15 days to meet demands
Article Text:
Pakistan's fuel crisis fears grow as petrol dealers threaten nationwide shutdown

Pakistan's petroleum dealers have threatened to shut down petrol pumps across the country if the government fails to introduce a monthly fuel pricing mechanism, giving authorities 15 days to address their demands, according to a report by Dawn.The Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association (PPDA) said frequent revisions in petroleum prices were causing serious financial difficulties for fuel retailers and rapidly depleting their working capital. Article Title: Lahore tops global pollution ranking again as AQI crosses 500, eight Pakistan cities among worst
Article Text:
Choking under state neglect: Lahore once again ranks world’s most polluted city as AQI breaches 500

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Lahore once again ranked as the world's most polluted major city on Sunday morning, with its Air Quality Index (AQI) reaching 538, placing it in the hazardous category, according to Pakistani daily Dawn. Eight cities in Punjab also featured among Pakistan's 10 most polluted urban centres, as severe smog continued to affect the province.Data from Swiss air quality monitoring platform IQAir showed Lahore at the top of the global major city ranking with an AQI of 538 between 9 am and 10 am. The reading exposed residents to severe health risks associated with hazardous air pollution.Karachi was further down the global ranking with an AQI of 180, followed by Cairo at 162.The pollution crisis extended beyond Lahore, with Kahna Nau in Lahore district recording the worst air quality in Pakistan at an AQI of 606. It was followed by Lahore at 538, Bahawalpur at 536, Sargodha at 392 and Gujranwala at 347, Dawn reported.Multan, Dera Ghazi Khan, Skardu, Faisalabad and Peshawar completed the list of the country's 10 most polluted cities.Lahore has repeatedly featured at the top of global pollution rankings in recent weeks.It recorded an AQI of 266 on Saturday evening, while the city had logged an hourly reading of 465 between 7 am and 8 am on Friday, as heavy smog affected several parts of Punjab.The continuing pollution has raised questions over the effectiveness of the Punjab administration's anti-smog measures. Lahore Traffic Police, however, has claimed that enforcement against vehicles contributing to air pollution has been stepped up.Chief Traffic Officer Syed Abdul Rahim Shirazi said on Saturday that traffic personnel had issued challan tickets to 14,653 vehicles emitting smoke. Action was also taken against 10,306 vehicles transporting sand, soil and other materials without tarpaulin covers. Police penalised 31,618 unfit and dilapidated vehicles and took action against 272,760 overloaded vehicles, he added.Separately, enforcement squads from the Punjab Environment Protection and Climate Change Department conducted 84,370 inspections of brick kilns across the province between January 1 and November 18, Dawn reported earlier this week. During this period, authorities demolished 1,429 kilns, sealed 968 and registered 1,248 FIRs against violators.Between September 1 and November 18, which covers the peak smog period, the department carried out 29,999 inspections, demolished 519 kilns, sealed 494 and registered 408 FIRs. It also imposed fines worth PKR 101.45 million.The scale of Pakistan's air pollution is also reflected in long-term data. The 2025 World Air Quality Report put the country's average PM2.5 concentration at 67.3 micrograms per cubic metre, nearly 14 times the World Health Organisation's annual guideline of 5 micrograms per cubic metre, Dawn reported.The report also placed Pakistan among the world's most polluted countries, with an average AQI of 156.Globally, indoor and outdoor air pollution together account for an estimated 8.1 million deaths annually, making air pollution the second-leading risk factor for mortality worldwide. Outdoor particulate matter alone is responsible for an estimated 4.7 million deaths.
Article Summary: Lahore once again ranks world’s most polluted city as AQI breaches 500. Eight cities in Punjab also featured among Pakistan's 10 most polluted urban centres. Lahore Traffic Police claims enforcement against vehicles contributing to air pollution has been stepped up.

United Nations high commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk has called for the immediate release of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan , raising concerns over his reported deteriorating health and detention conditions. Turk also urged the Pakistani government and opposition to de-escalate political tensions surrounding the case.In an interview with Christiane Amanpour on CNN, Turk said Khan's release could help build confidence between the government and the opposition.“I call for Imran Khan’s release. I call for his proper treatment, and I actually call for de-escalation. We need to diffuse the political tensions that are around this case, which means that a confidence-building measure between the opposition and the government could be his immediate release,” Turk said.His remarks come amid growing international concern over the health and treatment of the 74-year-old former prime minister, who remains in detention at Adiala Jail. It also said he had not been permitted to speak to his sons over the telephone since March 2026.Amnesty expressed concern over his reported solitary confinement and isolation from human contact, warning that the conditions could affect his physical and mental health. It said three of his sisters were detained on September 20 and 21 in connection with a planned Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf march to Islamabad.Khan had also issued an open letter to Pakistan's top judges on November 16, seeking urgent medical treatment and implementation of court orders. Article Title: 'Bloodshed in Karachi, Hyderabad': Why Bilawal Bhutto is opposing plan to redraw Pakistan's map
Article Text:
What is Pakistan's province-redrawing plan that has Bilawal Bhutto warning of bloodshed?

Why is Pakistan considering more provinces

Pakistan Peoples Party chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari has strongly opposed the proposal to divide Pakistan into multiple provinces, warning against any attempt to split Sindh by force.He cautioned that such a move could trigger violence and bloodshed in Karachi and Hyderabad, Pakistan-based Geo TV reported.The proposal to redraw Pakistan's political map has reportedly found support among several leaders in the country's power corridors, including army chief Asim Munir and defence minister Khawaja Asif Speaking at an event at the Karachi Press Club, Bilawal said any forced division of the province would create social divisions and push ordinary people towards violence, Geo TV reported.“If the province is divided by force, society will be divided, it will lead to enmity, ordinary people will take up arms, and the bloodshed will not be limited to a single death,” he said.The remarks come amid discussions in Pakistan about reorganising its administrative structure by dividing its four provinces into smaller units. Reports have suggested that army chief Asim Munir is considering a plan to create 12 to 15 provinces or reorganise the country into as many as 160 smaller administrative units to address governance challenges.The proposal has gained support from some senior ministers, but faces opposition from political parties, particularly over the possible division of Sindh, where the Bhutto-Zardari family and the PPP have a strong political base.Bilawal said the PPP was not opposed to creating new provinces but insisted that any such move must follow the wishes of the people and the constitutional process.“The PPP supports the creation of provinces in line with the wishes of the people, the Constitution and the law. Where we are opposing, it is over force and coercion. We do not want division through force,” he said.He also questioned suggestions that a referendum could be used to decide the issue, saying the Constitution already provided a procedure for creating new provinces.“If you are looking for an unconstitutional method, how can the PPP be with you?” he asked.Bilawal further said referendums in Pakistan's history had been used for undemocratic purposes. “It is not about a referendum, it is about intent,” he said.The proposal to increase the number of provinces from four to as many as 12 has gained momentum, with supporters arguing that smaller administrative units could improve governance and public services.Pakistan's defence minister Khawaja Asif has backed the idea, saying the country's growing population requires smaller provinces for more efficient administration.Speaking to Geo News, Asif said Pakistan could consider creating 12 provinces, provided their boundaries were based on administrative needs rather than linguistic, ethnic or political considerations.However, the proposal faces a major political challenge, with no consensus among leading parties, particularly over the possible division of Sindh.
Article Summary: Pakistan Peoples Party chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari has strongly opposed the proposal to divide Pakistan into multiple provinces. He cautioned that such a move could trigger violence and bloodshed in Karachi and Hyderabad. Reports have suggested that army chief Asim Munir is considering a plan to create 12 to 15 provinces.

Article Title: $135 billion in debt, still getting loans: Who is keeping Pakistan afloat, and why
Article Text:
Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and chief of defence forces Asim Munir (Reuters file photo)

What World Bank’s International Debt Report says about Pakistan

Pakistan’s economic challenges

China: Pakistan’s ‘all-weather’ friend

Why financial institutions continue lending to Pakistan

Can Pakistan actually repay its debt

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What happens if creditors stop lending to Pakistan

The World Bank ’s International Debt Report 2026 paints a stark picture of Pakistan’s growing external debt burden, showing that, as of 2025, Islamabad’s external debt had nearly doubled from its 2015 level.According to the report, Pakistan’s external debt stood at $135.1 billion last year, up from $68.7 billion in 2015, marking a 97% increase in just 10 years.Pakistan's mounting external debt presents a curious contradiction. Its economy continues to struggle, and its dependence on foreign financing remains substantial. Yet, despite these vulnerabilities, money continues to flow into the country from some of the world's most influential governments and financial institutions.The question, therefore, is not simply why Islamabad keeps borrowing, but why its creditors continue lending to a country whose ability to generate sufficient foreign exchange and meet its repayment obligations remains a source of concern.The $135.1 billion, which Pakistan owed as external debt, was up 4% from $129.9 billion in 2024. Of the 2025 debt, around $107.1 billion was public and publicly guaranteed debt, while the remainder included private-sector and short-term external obligations.Of Pakistan’s public and publicly guaranteed debt, nearly $57 billion is owed to multilateral creditors, while bilateral creditors account for over $42 billion, with the remainder owed to private creditors.Among individual creditors, China is Pakistan’s largest bilateral lender, accounting for $22.4 billion in debt. It is followed by the World Bank, with $19.2 billion, and the Asian Development Bank, with $16.83 billion, among other creditors.The report also highlighted the burden of debt repayments on Pakistan’s economy. In 2025, Islamabad spent an amount equivalent to 33% of its export earnings on servicing external debt, while total external debt stood at 34% of Gross National Income.The report, therefore, highlights the challenge facing Islamabad: managing its growing external debt while ensuring that its economy generates enough foreign exchange to meet repayment obligations.Continued lending does not necessarily mean Pakistan’s economy is healthy. Nor does its growing debt burden mean the country is on the verge of default.The latest economic indicators present a mixed picture.The World Bank estimates that Pakistan’s economy grew by 3.7% in FY26, up from 3.2% in the previous financial year. The fiscal deficit narrowed to 2.6% of GDP, while the current account recorded a small deficit of 0.1% of GDP. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) also reported that Pakistan’s gross foreign exchange reserves had risen to approximately $21.5 billion by the end of September 2025.These gains, however, are offset by continued economic challenges. Economic growth has not generated enough jobs for Pakistan’s growing workforce. About 3.5 million people enter the workforce every year, yet unemployment stood at 7% in 2024. While nearly 18 million new jobs have been created since 2018, most have been informal, low-paid or self-employment opportunities.Poverty, too, has increased, with the rate rising from 22% in 2018-19 to 29% in 2024-25. An estimated 70 million Pakistanis are now living in poverty.The future outlook also remains challenging. The World Bank projected Pakistan’s economy to grow by 3.8% in FY27, a marginal increase from the estimated 3.7% growth in FY26. Headline inflation was expected to rise to 8.2% in FY27 before easing to around 7%.The data therefore highlights the economic pressures Pakistan faces and is expected to confront in the coming years.China being Pakistan’s largest individual creditor is perhaps unsurprising. Beijing and Islamabad are, after all, each other’s “all-weather friends.”China’s investment in Pakistan has largely been channelled through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), the flagship project of Beijing’s ambitious Belt and Road Initiative. Under CPEC, Chinese investment in Pakistan is estimated at $62 billion over a period of 15 years.Another important feature of this economic relationship is loan rollover, under which a creditor extends the repayment period of existing loans instead of demanding immediate repayment. China has continued to roll over existing loans to Pakistan, providing Islamabad temporary relief from its foreign currency obligations without reducing its overall debt.With Pakistan struggling to repay its Chinese loans, what explains Beijing's willingness to not only continue providing financial support to Islamabad but also roll over existing loans?Sushant Sareen, senior fellow at the Observer Research Foundation and an expert on Pakistan, attributed Beijing's continued support to the “strategic relationship” between the two countries.“It’s not just about an economic relationship between them. I think one of the reasons why the Chinese keep bailing Pakistan out and give them money is because of the strategic relationship that exists between them,” Sareen told The Times of India.Even CPEC, he added, was China’s plan to “prop up” Pakistan’s economy and make it more efficient and productive.Ultimately, the question is whether Pakistan can generate enough foreign exchange to service its growing debt, even with continued support from China.That Beijing is Islamabad’s largest creditor comes as little surprise. However, multilateral institutions such as the IMF and the World Bank also continue to play an important role in financing Pakistan.Since joining the IMF in 1950, Pakistan has received around two dozen bailout packages. Most recently, in October, the IMF agreed to release another $1.21 billion under its ongoing loan and sustainability programmes, subject to Executive Board approval.In a recent YouTube interview, former IMF chief economist Gita Gopinath was asked why the lender continues to bail out Pakistan despite concerns over its ability to repay its loans.Gopinath explained that the IMF’s role is to help countries facing economic crises and that it cannot simply walk away from them.She also emphasised that the IMF's decisions are taken by its member countries, including India. The decision to extend a loan, therefore, rests with the membership rather than the IMF's management.Sareen echoed this view.“Pakistan is a member of the IMF. It is the IMF’s job to bail out countries which are facing balance of payments problems,” he said.He, however, pointed out that political considerations could also influence the IMF's lending decisions.“India holds slightly over 2% vote share and that's not big enough to veto the loan. The Americans with 16% or 17% stake can actually do that, because with 15% you can veto any IMF loan. And clearly the Americans don't want to turn the screws on the Pakistanis. So, yes, to some extent it is a political decision to give money to Pakistan,” he argued.Sareen noted, however, that overall, the IMF largely operates within its economic mandate.Taken together, Islamabad's repeated reliance on the IMF underlines the extent to which its economy depends on external financial support.Pakistan's total external debt of around $135 billion does not mean the entire amount is due for repayment immediately. The debt has accumulated over several years, with repayments spread across different periods.The extent of Pakistan's reliance on fresh borrowing is evident from the figures. In FY26, it received $16.16 billion in external loans, while repaying around $14.44 billion in external public debt, including $11.20 billion in principal and $3.24 billion in interest, according to the ministry of economic affairs.The key question, therefore, is whether Islamabad can generate enough foreign exchange to meet these repayment obligations while managing its other economic needs.Sareen argued that the bigger challenge for Pakistan was not repaying its entire debt, but servicing it — having enough foreign exchange to meet repayment and interest obligations as they fall due.“Pakistans' problem is that they're not earning the kind of foreign exchange they require to service that debt. And the debt which they're taking on is increasing virtually every year. But for now, they're managing to tide it over. They managed to avoid default, but at a very high price,” he said.The challenge for Islamabad, therefore, is not just to keep securing loans, but to build an economy capable of meeting its repayment obligations without repeatedly relying on external support.Pakistan is often described as a country facing economic collapse and the risk of disintegration. Its continued dependence on external financing raises an important question: what would happen if lenders stopped extending fresh loans to Islamabad?The withdrawal of support from its lenders would not automatically push Pakistan into default or close to disintegration. Rather, it would face severe economic difficulties.Sareen warned that a default could trigger severe economic hardship, with Pakistan potentially spending three to four years trying to stabilise its economy and regain access to the international financial system. During this period, it could struggle to maintain imports and deal with foreign exchange shortages.But Pakistan continues to stay afloat — with support from international institutions, as well as countries whose financial assistance is shaped by strategic interests. Lending decisions also have a political dimension, with the interests and influence of powerful member countries playing a role.For now, creditors continue to extend financial support, even as concerns over Islamabad's ability to repay its debt persist.
Article Summary: Pakistan's external debt stood at $135.1 billion last year, up from $68.7 billion in 2015. China is Pakistan’s largest bilateral lender, accounting for $22.4 billion in debt. Pakistan spent an amount equivalent to 33% of its export earnings on servicing external debt.

The sons of imprisoned former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan have accused authorities of subjecting their father to prolonged physical and mental torture in Adiala Jail, warning that he could die in custody without urgent medical intervention.In an interview with Sky News's Mark Austin, Sulaiman Isa Khan and Kasim Khan expressed concern over the deteriorating health of the 74-year-old Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder, alleging that he was being kept in solitary confinement for 22 to 23 hours a day, with little human contact and no access to independent medical care."We can see the path that this is taking. It's inevitable that eventually he will die in this cell. It's at a point where they've instructed the guards not to even speak to him while he's in the cell just to, you know, maintain pressure and mental pressure on him," they added.The brothers said authorities had failed to implement an August 18 Supreme Court order directing that Khan be shifted to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for medical examination and treatment. The order had also called for increased family access, including regular telephone conversations with his sons."Nothing's changed at all, despite an order from the Supreme Court back in August for him to be taken and treated at a private hospital called Shifa International, and for increased family access to his family, calls with us, regular calls with us. "I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he said.However, Pakistan's cabinet minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed Khan's claims, saying he had received regular medical attention and had been taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad eight times for examinations. Article Title: Former Pakistan army officer is new BLA chief

In a major organisational shift, Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) has elevated its senior commander Rehman Gul to the post of commander-in-chief. Sources said his elevation carried symbolic weight given his past as a former captain in Pakistan army’s 19 Frontier Force (FF) Regiment.In 2010, Gul deserted the army, citing atrocities against civilians, and joined Aslam Baloch’s BLA, leaving the military brass flummoxed. Prior to assuming the top role, Gul served on the command council and led the Majeed Brigade, BLA’s operational wing which specialises in suicide bombings.Having graduated as a battalion senior major, Gul previously held military postings in Kotli in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir as well as North and South Waziristan, where he took part in military operations.The announcement also dispels earlier reports from the Pakistani military, which had declared Gul dead last year, a claim BLA didn’t validate. Adding a sensitive dynamic to the situation, sources indicate that Gul’s younger brother currently serves as a Major in the Pakistan army’s Signals Corps. Observers suggest that having a former military officer at the helm amplifies narratives of internal disillusionment among security personnel regarding state crackdowns and civilian casualties in Balochistan.The leadership transition, confirmed through a statement from group spokesperson Jeeyand Baloch on Nov 14, follows a unanimous vote by the outfit’s senior command council. The move comes just days after the announcement that Bashir Zeb was stepping down as chief.There was also uncertainty surrounding Zeb’s successor after the group said last week that Zeb was transferring all powers to the command council. While pro-Pak military social media accounts circulated rumours of Zeb having been poisoned by a confidante and being killed in Afghanistan, sources described them as false.

Bangladesh’s renewed political unrest over former prime minister Sheikh Hasina ’s planned return has spilled into a wave of arson and attacks on institutions linked to her political rivals.Grameen Bank, founded by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, who led the interim government after Hasina’s ouster, has been among the targets, with the bank recording 100 incidents of arson or attempted arson at its branches and offices since November 10.The bank’s Internal Audit and Compliance Division report, dated November 24, lists incidents across the country. It includes an attack on the Patgati branch in Tungipara, which was targeted twice, on November 10 and 15.In the latest incidents, attackers hurled petrol bombs at branches in Lalmonirhat and Tangail in the early hours of Tuesday. At the Patgram branch in Lalmonirhat, a petrol bomb was thrown at the veranda around 2.45am. The night guard and branch manager raised the alarm, forcing the attackers to flee. The report said there was no major damage, though a halogen light temporarily went out.At the Shashanpur branch in Gopalpur, Tangail, another petrol bomb was thrown around 2am, damaging the branch’s signboard.The tally has risen from 97 incidents recorded in the bank’s previous report, dated November 23. It includes attempted attacks that caused little or no damage.The attacks have also disrupted operations and damaged records at several branches.At the Ulpur branch in Gopalganj, attackers set fire to the office on November 15, burning collection sheets and damaging a table. They also broke CCTV equipment and took a hard disk, according to the bank’s incident record.In another attack on November 23, two people poured petrol near the main gate of the Keroa Raipur branch in Noakhali and set it alight. A night guard and a peon extinguished the fire before it spread. Police later examined CCTV footage and arrested one person, the report said.An earlier attack on the Kashiani branch in Gopalganj on November 18 caused extensive damage. Branch manager Solaiman Morol told Al Jazeera that around a dozen men arrived carrying machetes, petrol and tools to break locks. They looted the office and tried to cut open its vault with a grinder.The attackers took about 40 sacks of vouchers and other documents and burned them, Morol said. They also stole office furniture and equipment. The branch has been unable to resume normal operations, while staff have received threats and customers have expressed concern about their deposits and loan records.Morol said the attackers claimed that destroying the records would mean borrowers no longer had to repay their loans.The latest report came a day after Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus appealed to the international community to help stop what he described as a “calculated campaign of arson and terror” against the bank.Yunus said branches had been attacked with petrol bombs almost daily since the beginning of November, often accompanied by slogans associated with the Awami League, the party of ousted former prime minister Sheikh Hasina.He called for those responsible to be brought to justice and urged supporters of the bank around the world to help stop the attacks. He also said Grameen Bank had asked the Ministry of Home Affairs for stronger security.The violence has raised concerns over the safety of the bank’s employees and borrowers. Grameen Bank has around 21,000 employees and about 11 million borrowers, most of them women, according to figures cited by Yunus and the bank.The institution is owned 90% by its borrower-members, with the government holding the remaining 10%. The attacks therefore threaten not only the bank’s operations but also the financial security of millions of rural borrowers who rely on it for credit and savings.Bangladesh’s government has blamed the Awami League for the attacks. The violence has come amid renewed political activity by Hasina’s supporters, months after she was ousted in August 2024 and Yunus stepped down as chief adviser.Political analysts cited by Al Jazeera said Grameen Bank had become a symbol of Yunus and a target for supporters of the former prime minister. Some viewed the attacks as an attempt to demonstrate that the Awami League still had a presence on the streets, despite being barred from electoral politics.The government has rejected suggestions that it is unable to contain the violence.Police headquarters told Al Jazeera that eight cases had been filed and eight people arrested in connection with the attacks.Grameen Bank managing director Sarder Akhter Hamed said police had responded when the bank sought help and had sometimes warned it of possible attacks. However, he said staff had largely been left to remain alert and protect themselves.The attacks have also drawn alarm from human rights organisations, which warned that the violence puts bank workers and members at risk and threatens the economic rights of women entrepreneurs and rural communities.
Article Summary: Grameen Bank has recorded 100 incidents of arson or attempted arson at its branches and offices since November 10. Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus has appealed to the international community to help stop what he described as a “calculated campaign of arson and terror” against the bank.

TOI Correspondent from Dhaka:

‘No plane, copter, bus, car or rickshaw for Hasina’

Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina on Tuesday declared she plans to head home on December 16, when the country celebrates its independence from Pakistan, only to be met with yet another sign that the governing BNP is not quite keen on the Awami League boss's return, notwithstanding their declared intent to carry out the death sentence awarded to her.Following through on her earlier statement that she would be home by the year-end and was ready to face consequences, Hasina asked Dhaka to arrange her air travel from India on national carrier Biman Bangladesh, the former PM's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali said in a statement.Hasina's 'December 16' announcement - the first time she gave a date of return - triggered strong reactions in Dhaka, with state minister for foreign affairs Humaiun Kobir Tuesday saying that "she can only be brought back through extradition, in handcuffs" and stressing "reality and desire are two different things".Everyone knows that Hasina is a terrorist and that terrorism is sponsored by her from New Delhi,” Kobir told a news conference at the foreign ministry.Not many were, however, impressed, considering that the extradition route is used to bring back those who may not be willing to return. “Have you ever heard of a situation where the accused herself is willing to return to face trial, yet the receiving country insists on extradition, especially when the extradition process is unlikely to succeed or, at the very least, could take a long time? Does that make any sense at all?”Awami League functionary and former cabinet minister Mohammad Ali Arafat asked.Shama Obaed Islam, also a state minister for foreign affairs, said that “govt has not made any arrangements with anyone to send a plane, helicopter, bus, car, or rickshaw. Is that clear?”. She, while addressing the presser, said all Bangladesh missions abroad are considered “Bangladesh territory”, and Hasina would face arrest if she appears at any of those missions.PM’s information and broadcasting adviser Zahed Ur Rahman said govt had no communication with Hasina over her return and was holding discussions with India on the issue. “Let me tell you clearly... if this particular individual, or any other convicted person, returns, they will be treated as accused; they will be arrested immediately and sent to jail — to the central jail. There will be no deviation from this,” Shama Obaed said, referring to a special tribunal sentencing Hasina to death in 2025. Kobir said the reality is that a terrorist will never be allowed to come back other than through extradition. “The desire may be there...coming on foot or by flight. No, she is not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs,” he said.
Article Summary: Hasina asked Dhaka to arrange her air travel from India on national carrier Biman Bangladesh, the former PM's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali said in a statement.
